issues.title: discuss use cases for when pseudonymity would be used with hwk
issues.author: dickhardt

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Addressed (commit on `main`, §Pseudonymous Access in Privacy Considerations). Documents when pseudonymous keying (`scheme=hwk` / `scheme=jkt-jwt` — key-only, no `aauth:` identity) is appropriate: privacy-preserving access, sybil-resistance/rate-limiting without identification, ephemeral/unenrolled agents, capability-style access, and hardware-anchored continuity. Clarifies that pseudonymous != anonymous (a key still links a holder's requests at one resource — fresh keys are needed for unlinkability), and that resources requiring attributable identity MUST reject pseudonymous keys and require an `identity` scheme. Closing.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
**Correction to the earlier resolution.** On review we decided the opposite: AAuth does **not** support pseudonymous access. The Agent Token Acquisition section already mandates that every participant hold an agent token, so the agent token is AAuth's minimum credential — there is no AAuth flow that uses a bare `hwk` key.

`hwk` entered the discussion from the underlying HTTP Signature Keys spec (which defines `pseudonym` schemes `hwk`/`jkt-jwt` alongside the `identity` schemes `jwt`/`jwks_uri`); this issue's original framing presupposed AAuth used it. It doesn't.

Changes (commit on `main`):
- Removed the §Pseudonymous Access section added earlier.
- §Keying Material now states AAuth uses only the **identity** schemes; `hwk` is unused and `jkt-jwt` appears only in the AP's key-refresh ceremony (bootstrap), never for protocol access.
- Fixed the DPoP comparison to start progressive requirements from verified agent identity.

So the answer to 'when would pseudonymity be used with hwk' is: **not in AAuth** — the agent token is the floor. Closing as resolved.

issues.title: not all platforms (browsers) provide easy access to components for HTTP Message Signing profile
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body: Which components are required likely is a SHOULD rather than MUST -- and provide rationale when it is not done.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Addressed (commit on `main`, §Covered Components). Decision: **keep the four base components MUST** and add the rationale you asked for.

The browser-access concern doesn't bite for the mandated set — `@method`, `@authority`, `@path`, and `signature-key` are all app-known at signing time in a browser `fetch`. The components that *are* awkward on constrained platforms (e.g., `content-digest` over the body, or auto-added headers) are already in the **MAY / additional** bucket, learned via `required_input`. Each of the four closes a concrete replay vector (method/host/path/key substitution), so relaxing them would lower the security floor with no real portability gain. Added rationale spelling out what each prevents. Closing.

issues.title: Non-repudiation and key rotation: audit trail considerations?
issues.author: christian-posta
issues.body:
Agent delegates use ephemeral keys, and agent servers can rotate their JWKS. The spec focuses on proving message authenticity at request time where the entity signing the message holds the private key bound to the agent identity. But how should adopters think about audit and non-repudiation after the fact?

Once keys rotate out of JWKS, old signatures become unverifiable. The only persistent identifiers are `agent` and `sub` (agent delegate), but these don't help you cryptographically prove "agent X signed request Y at time T" after key rotation.

Is this intentional (privacy-preserving by design)?

Should the spec offer guidance for deployments that need audit trails?

Are there recommended patterns (e.g., resources archiving tokens at verification time, key transparency logs)?

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Good points. I think a transparency log is a good direction to explore for this.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: @christian-posta what are your thoughts on recommending a transparency log?

comments.author: nickgamb-strata
comments.body:
Our trajectory hash chaining proposal in PR #10 addresses part of this.

The core idea: each audit entry in the mission log chains to the previous via `SHA-256(prev_hash | action | params | result)`, seeded from the mission's s256. This gives you a tamper-evident execution log whose integrity is verifiable independently of key material - you don't need the signing key to verify the chain, just the s256 anchor and the ordered entries.

This doesn't solve the full non-repudiation problem (you still can't prove agent X signed request Y after key rotation), but it does give you a cryptographic guarantee that the audit trail hasn't been modified, reordered, or had entries removed after the fact. If the PS records the chain at verification time, you get durable audit integrity even as keys rotate out.

For deployments that need stronger non-repudiation, the hash chain could be extended with a receipt pattern - the PS returns a signed receipt for each audit entry that the agent or a third party can archive. That way you have both chain integrity (our proposal) and point-in-time attestation (receipts signed with a PS key that has a longer lifecycle than agent keys).

comments.author: jagmarques
comments.body:
Two patterns worth separating in the spec, because they solve different threat models.

Pattern A, archive-at-verification. The resource server persists each verified token (or a digest of it plus the JWKS snapshot used to verify) at the moment of acceptance. This gives you "we verified X under key Y at time T" forever, but it pushes the trust to the RS log: a malicious or compromised RS can rewrite history. Cheap, common, weak against insider threat.

Pattern B, transparency log inclusion. After verification, the RS submits a canonical hash of the request (RFC 8785 or whatever canonicalization the spec settles on) plus the verifying JWK thumbprint to an append-only log. Verifiers later get a Merkle inclusion proof tying the signed request to a fixed log root. Sigstore's Rekor and the certificate-transparency RFC 6962 / 9162 designs are the well-trodden paths. This is the right answer if you want non-repudiation that survives RS compromise, JWKS rotation, and key revocation.

Pattern C, RFC 3161 timestamps over the request hash. Cheaper than running a log, gives you "this signature existed at this time" without needing the original key to be live. Doesn't catch equivocation, doesn't give you set membership, but it's the lightest-weight option and it composes with A and B.

Trajectory hash chaining (PR #10) is orthogonal to all three. It proves ordering and tamper-evidence within a single mission, but it does not prove that the chain head was witnessed by anyone outside the agent server. Without an external anchor (signed checkpoint, log entry, timestamp), a chain can be silently truncated at the tail; you only catch mid-chain deletions.

Suggested spec move: keep AAuth itself silent on archival, but add a non-normative section "Long-term verification" that names these three patterns and notes that signature validity has a defined lifetime equal to the JWKS retention window unless one of A/B/C is layered on. Implementers will reach for the wrong pattern without that nudge.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Addressed (commit on `main`, §Non-Repudiation and Audit After Key Rotation). Answers the three questions:

1. **Intentional?** Partly by design — AAuth provides request-time authentication (proof-of-possession), not long-term non-repudiation; short-lived keys + directed identifiers limit long-term linkability.
2. **Guidance?** Yes — deployments needing durable audit should capture evidence **at verification time** (while the key is still in the JWKS), not rely on re-verification after rotation.
3. **Patterns?** Archive the request+signature+`Signature-Key`+trusted timestamp; optional JWKS-entry (`kid`+JWK) snapshot; RFC 3161 timestamping or tamper-evident/transparency logs; index records by `(iss,sub)` and `jti`. Flags the privacy tradeoff of archiving signatures/keys. Closing.

issues.title: Should clarify the HTTP message signature steps in 9.10 Token Exchange
issues.author: christian-posta
issues.body:
For the scenario:

Agent 1 --> Agent 2 --> Resource 

Agent 1 passes an Auth Token... and for Agent 2 to call resource, it needs to pass the following to Resource's Auth Server:

- resource token
- Agent 2's "upstream" token, aka the token Agent 1 passes to Agent 2.

But it's not clear how the Auth Server involved in the token exchange is supposed to verify the signature. 

> The upstream auth token MUST be presented via the Signature-Key header using sig=jwt;jwt="<upstream-auth-token>".

Which signature? The upstream jwt is signed by Agent 1 (ie, jwt.cnf is Agent 1's public key). The JWT itself is signed by the Auth Server of Agent 2.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
I think this is a mistake in that version of the doc 

the upstream auth token is a parameter in the call to the AS2 token endpoint -- the signature-key would be signed by the agent and include either an agent token or the jwks_uri

comments.author: christian-posta
comments.body: Excellent, that's how i implemented it in my POCs. Thanks!

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Resolved by the current call-chaining design (commit on `main`, §Call Chaining / §Upstream Token Verification).

Your confusion was real **for the old §9.10 design**, where the upstream auth token was presented via `Signature-Key` — so it was ambiguous whether the AS verified Agent 1's key (the upstream token's `cnf`) or Agent 2's. The redesign removes the ambiguity:

- `upstream_token` is now a **body parameter**, not presented via `Signature-Key`.
- The intermediary (Agent 2 / Resource 1) signs the downstream request with **its own** key, presenting **its own** agent token via `Signature-Key`.
- The `upstream_token` is the auth token previously issued **to the intermediary** — its `aud` is the intermediary and its `cnf` is the intermediary's key — and serves only as proof of the upstream authorization.

So the signature the recipient verifies is always the intermediary's, over its own key. Added an explicit sentence saying exactly this. Closing.

comments.author: nickgamb-strata
comments.body:
Interesting thread - we hit a similar tension from the governance side.

We've been implementing AAuth Mission Contracts for MCP tool governance (PR #10 has our proposed extensions). One pattern that emerged was "mission template discovery" - the PS publishes structured templates describing common mission types with suggested tools and constraints.

The parallel here: when an agent's intent spans what a resource would naturally partition into separate authorization bundles, who resolves that - the resource, the agent, or the PS?

In our implementation, the PS. The agent proposes a mission in terms of what it wants to accomplish, and the PS maps that to the appropriate authorization requests. If a mission needs `listEvents` + `createEvent` across different R3 docs, the PS handles multiple token exchanges behind the scenes - the agent just sees one approved mission.

That aligns with Dick's leaning toward "one doc, many operations" or "split into multiple token exchanges" - the PS can abstract that split from the agent.

On the `type` field: in our template model, each template groups operations by intent rather than API surface. "Account Inquiry" vs "Account Management" rather than "read" vs "write." Worth considering whether R3 `type` should reflect the resource's access model or the user's intent model, since those don't always align.

Happy to share more from the implementation side.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Clarified in the R3 spec (commit on branch `address-open-issues`, §Operations Spanning Multiple Definitions).

A single resource/auth token carries exactly one `r3_uri`/`r3_s256`. When the requested operations span more than one of the resource's internal R3 definitions, the resource **composes a single R3 document** covering the union of operations, with a combined `display`, and serves it at a fresh content-addressed `r3_uri` (built on the fly, bytes persisted so the hash is stable). Content-addressing means an identical operation set reduces to the same hash and can be reused.

For your example: the resource maps `listEvents` + `createEvent` into one composed document carrying both operations; the resource token references that one document. The agent only ever sees one opaque `r3_uri`/`r3_s256`.

issues.title: auth_token lifetime: add recommended TTL bound (or guidance)
issues.author: rohanharikr
issues.body:
The protocol bounds `agent_token` (SHOULD NOT exceed 24 hours, §5.2.2) and `resource_token` (SHOULD NOT exceed 5 minutes, §6.6.1), but `auth_token` lifetime is silent. The only signal is an example value `expires_in: 3600` in §7.1.4, which is illustrative.

This affects revocation latency planning — the worst-case window between a PS revoking a binding and the agent losing access at an RS is bounded by the auth_token TTL. Without spec guidance, implementations will diverge.

Suggestion: add a SHOULD upper bound (e.g. ≤1 hour) or guidance text on trade-offs (revocation responsiveness vs PS bootstrap traffic).

comments.author: rohanharikr
comments.body:
On re-reading the spec, the bound exists at line 1538 (§ Auth Token Structure):

> Auth tokens MUST NOT have a lifetime exceeding 1 hour.

This is a stronger constraint than the SHOULD I suggested. Closing — issue based on a misread of the spec.

issues.title: Verifiers should check issuer matches the URL metadata was fetched from
issues.author: rohanharikr
issues.body:
[RFC 8414](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8414) makes this normative for OAuth Authorization Server Metadata: when a verifier fetches a metadata document, the `issuer` claim inside MUST match the URL it was fetched from (less the `/.well-known/...` suffix).

AAuth doesn't appear to require this check. Without it, a "host-poisoned metadata" attack is possible against permissive RSes — an attacker hosts metadata at their own domain claiming to be a different issuer, and an RS that follows the metadata's `jwks_uri` could end up trusting attacker-controlled keys to verify tokens claiming the impersonated issuer.

Suggestion: add normative language requiring verifiers to check `metadata.issuer === <top-level URL fetched from>` and reject on mismatch. Could live in metadata-handling sections for agent servers, resource servers, and person servers (all three publish well-knowns).

comments.author: jagmarques
comments.body:
Strong +1 on making this normative. The host-poisoned metadata path is real, and it's the kind of bug RS implementers will skip if the spec doesn't tell them to check.

One thing worth nailing down: the comparison should be on the canonicalized issuer URL (no trailing slash, lowercase scheme/host), otherwise interop breaks on subtle differences. Verifiers also need to repeat the check on every metadata refresh, not just first fetch, since rotated metadata could swap the issuer claim.

If you go this route, the language probably wants to say "the verifier MUST reject if the `issuer` does not match the URL the metadata was retrieved from (after normalization)". That phrasing is unambiguous enough that an implementer can write a test from it.

issues.title: R3 hash verification: add explicit "no canonicalization, hash bytes as served" guidance
issues.author: rohanharikr
issues.body:
The R3 spec currently mandates RFC 8785 canonical JSON serialization for the hash:

> "computed as the SHA-256 hash of the canonical JSON serialization ([@!RFC8785]) of the R3 document" (§ R3 hash)
> "Compute the SHA-256 hash of the fetched document using canonical JSON serialization ([@!RFC8785])" (§ R3 fetch verification)

Suggestion: remove the canonicalization requirement. Hash the bytes the resource serves, not a re-canonicalized form.

Rationale:
- Canonicalization adds an implementation dependency (RFC 8785 libraries, edge cases) that's hard to get right.
- The resource is the authoritative source of bytes — its serialization IS the document.
- Pattern: serialize once at the RS, persist those bytes, serve them verbatim. Verifier hashes received bytes directly.

Practical implications:
- Replace "canonical JSON serialization" with "the bytes returned by the resource"
- Add implementer guidance: serialize once, store, serve verbatim — re-serialization between hash computation and serving will break the chain
- RSes that build R3 documents on the fly need to persist serialized bytes (e.g. KV) rather than re-build/re-serialize per request

comments.author: jagmarques
comments.body:
There is a real tension here, but I think the spec should keep canonicalization and instead tighten the implementation guidance.

The "hash bytes as served" pattern works as long as the bytes are produced exactly once and never re-serialized. In practice it breaks in three places:

1. Any HTTP intermediary that decompresses, re-compresses, or alters Content-Encoding will change the served bytes without changing the document. CDNs, reverse proxies, and even some logging middleware do this.
2. JSON libraries with non-deterministic key ordering or different float-formatting between encode and re-encode will silently break verification on the verifier side if it ever round-trips. It does, eventually, somewhere in a multi-team deployment.
3. RS implementations that build R3 documents from a database row do not have authoritative bytes; they have a record. They have to canonicalize at construction time anyway.

RFC 8785 was written specifically to solve "two implementations, same JSON value, different bytes". Dropping it pushes the canonicalization burden into operations, where it gets handled inconsistently.

A middle path that I think actually matches the proposal's intent: keep RFC 8785 as the canonical form, but add a normative requirement that the RS persists the canonical bytes at issuance time (along with the signature), and serves those exact bytes on subsequent fetches. The verifier hashes received bytes directly, with no re-canonicalization. The canonicalization happens once, in one place, with one library, at the moment the document is signed.

That gives you the implementation simplicity the proposal wants ("verifier hashes received bytes") without losing the interoperability guarantee that RFC 8785 buys you. The only thing the spec needs to add is that the RS must not re-build or re-serialize the document between hash computation and serving, which is what the proposal already says.

Worth checking if anyone is hitting RFC 8785 edge cases in practice (BigInt, unpaired surrogates, -0 vs 0, locale-dependent number formatting in older Java/Go libs) before pulling it. If yes, narrowing the JSON profile is more useful than removing canonicalization.

issues.title: Discovery: allow following HTTP redirects within the same eTLD+1
issues.author: rohanharikr
issues.body:
Many real-world deployments would benefit from letting users specify a top-level domain (e.g. `hello.coop`) instead of a service-specific subdomain (e.g. `person.hello.coop`) when configuring an issuer. The metadata document can live at the subdomain, and a redirect from the top-level well-known fetches it.

Suggestion: define behavior for HTTP redirects during discovery:
- Redirects within the same eTLD+1 (e.g. `hello.coop` → `person.hello.coop`) MUST be followed
- The `issuer === fetched-URL` check (#12) is performed against the **redirected** URL, not the original
- Redirects across eTLD+1 boundaries SHOULD NOT be followed (or require explicit opt-in)

This lets `https://hello.coop/.well-known/aauth-person.json` redirect to `https://person.hello.coop/.well-known/aauth-person.json` and have the `issuer` claim be `https://person.hello.coop`. Both URLs work as discovery entry points.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Closing as won't-fix-via-redirects.

The implementation PRs (#18, reworked as #40) proposed following same-eTLD+1 redirects and validating the metadata against the post-redirect URL. That's the wrong trust model: AAuth's metadata discovery is a machine verifier resolving an issuer it already holds (token `iss`, agent token `ps` claim, or `aud`), so letting a redirect move the verifier from `person.hello.coop` to `person2.hello.coop` means trusting a different server's keys. Same eTLD+1 != same security principal.

This also inverts RFC 8414 §3.3 / OIDC Discovery §4.3, which both validate `issuer` against the original issuer-derived URL and do not permit redirects to change the issuer. See #40 for the full reasoning.

The underlying convenience goal — let a user type `hello.coop` and land on the canonical issuer `person.hello.coop` — is a config-time / UX hint-resolution concern, not protocol-verifier behavior. If we want to support it, it belongs in a one-time setup step that surfaces the resolved canonical issuer to the user, not in token-verification redirect-following. Open a fresh issue scoped that way if/when we pursue it.

The issuer-match check itself (the safe, precedent-aligned half) lives on in #39 (closes #12).

issues.title: Terminology cleanup: fix wording where spec text says "this URL is an agent" instead of "agent server"
issues.author: rohanharikr

The Terminology section already defines `agent`, `agent server`, `agent_token` etc. correctly. But there are spots in the spec body where prose reads as if a URL is itself "an agent" — when what's meant is that the URL identifies an *agent server*.

issues.title: Add `class` claim for grouping agent instances
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Background

AAuth's per-instance agent identity (`aauth:local@domain`) gives each runtime its own identifier and signing key — great for per-instance authorization, revocation, and audit. But there's no first-class way to group instances of the same product.

A user installing Planner today has to consent to each Planner instance separately. A new install or container restart triggers re-consent. There's no way to say "I trust any Planner instance from vendor.example."

## Proposal

Add an OPTIONAL `class` claim to the agent token.

```json
{
  "iss":   "https://vendor.example",
  "sub":   "aauth:planner.7f3c@vendor.example",
  "cnf":   { "jwk": ... },
  "class": "planner"
}
```

**Semantics:**

- `class` is an opaque string defined by the AP.
- A class is identified by the tuple `(iss, class)`. Verifiers MUST scope all class comparisons to that tuple.
- Comparison is exact string equality.

**Where it lives:**

- Only in the agent token. NOT copied to auth tokens.

**Who enforces it:**

- The PS only. PS uses class for grant matching. When a user consents at class granularity, the PS records `(user, iss, class) → {scopes, ...}`. Future instances of the same class match the existing grant without re-consent.

**Storage is implementation choice.** PSes can synthesize an internal key like `https://vendor.example/planner` for indexing, or use any other scheme. The wire format stays minimal.

**No hierarchy.** Class strings are flat. APs may use any internal naming convention but the protocol does exact equality only.

## Rationale

### Why class at all

Per-instance identity without a category concept means per-instance consent — too fine-grained for users in practice. Every major AI agent identity system has converged on having a class-like concept:

- **Microsoft Foundry / Entra Agent ID**: agent identity blueprints "establish the category of agent through type classification" (e.g., "Contoso Sales Agent"). Each agent identity is an instance of a blueprint. `InheritDelegatedPermissions` lets instances inherit permissions from the blueprint to "reduce consent complexity for multi-instance scenarios."
- **Google OAuth (cross-client identity)**: project-wide consent — "when a user has granted access to a particular scope to any client ID in a project, the grant indicates the user's trust in the whole application."
- **Karl McGuinness's `client_instance_assertion` draft**: separates `client_id` (logical class) from `sub` (instance).
- **Auth0, Okta, Ping**: all building agent identity products with class-like categorization.

AAuth's `class` claim is the same pattern in our terminology: AP labels what kind of agent an instance is.

### Why flat (no hierarchy)

Three reasons:

1. **No production system uses hierarchical class.** Microsoft blueprints are flat. Google projects are flat. Karl's `client_id` is flat. A hierarchical AAuth class would put us in a club of one.

2. **Hierarchy use cases are covered by other primitives.** "User consents to /planner; should cover sub-agents" — sub-agents get authorization via parent delegation, not class match. "Reject sub-agents for sensitive scope" — handled by the `act != ∅` check, not class depth. "Resource policy by class subtree" — class is PS-only; resources don't see it.

3. **Implementation cost vs. benefit is poor.** Hierarchy requires prefix-matching DB queries, normalization rules, depth concept, "most specific match wins" semantics. Flat equality is one query.

### Why PS-only

The PS is the consent/grant authority. Class exists for consent grouping. Pushing class into auth tokens is propagating an input that's already been consumed by the only party that uses it.

## Open questions

1. Does anyone have a real cross-deployment use case for hierarchical class that the flat model can't express?
2. When `class` is omitted, the PS treats the agent purely by agent identifier (today's behavior). Good?

## References

- [Microsoft Foundry Agent Identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/agent-identity)
- [Google Cross-client Identity](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/cross-client-identity)
- [Karl McGuinness — client-instance-assertion](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-mcguinness-oauth-client-instance-assertion/)
- [Auth0 for AI Agents](https://auth0.com/ai)
- [Okta agentic identity](https://www.okta.com/products/govern-ai-agent-identity/)

comments.body:

There is an issue with mulit-tenant APs -- an agent with a class can act for any tenant with the scope -- which is not what a tenant of the AP wants. 

## Multi-tenant APs: add `tenant` to scope class grants

Class as defined here works cleanly when the AP is per-user or per-tenant (`alice.vendor.example`, `customer.vendor.example`) — `iss` is enough to scope the grant. It does **not** work for genuinely multi-tenant APs (`vendor.example` serving everyone): Alice's `aauth:planner.X@vendor.example` and Bob's `aauth:planner.Y@vendor.example` both match `(iss=vendor.example, class=planner)`, and the PS has no way to tell them apart without per-instance enrollment — which is the friction class is meant to remove.

The fix is to add an OPTIONAL `tenant` claim to the agent token. This doesn't break the AP-knows-nothing-about-users property: `tenant` is something the AP already manages publicly (orgs, customer accounts, billing scopes).

### Shape

```json
{
  "iss":    "https://vendor.example",
  "sub":    "aauth:planner.7f3c@vendor.example",
  "cnf":    { "jwk": ... },
  "classes": [ "planner", "research"],
  "tenant": "acme"
}
```

### Grant types

The PS already scopes everything to the person, so grants within a person's PS state come in three shapes:

- `agent_id` — per-instance grant (today's behavior)
- `(AP, class)` — class grant for per-user / per-tenant APs
- `(AP, class, tenant)` — class grant for multi-tenant APs

### Net delta to the proposal

- Add OPTIONAL `tenant` claim to the agent token, semantics by reference to the existing auth-token claim and OIDC.Enterprise.
- Define class grant key as `(AP, class)` or `(AP, class, tenant)` depending on AP topology, alongside the existing per-`agent_id` grant.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
## Class token: separate AP-signed artifact, presented only to the PS

With earlier proposals, we were leaking the tenant and classes to the resource ... 

Reworking the proposal to keep `class` and `tenant` out of the agent token entirely. The agent token stays exactly as it is today — no class, no tenant, no leakage of routing metadata to resources.

Class becomes a separate AP-issued artifact: the **class token**.

### Shape

A class token is an AP-signed JWT carrying:

- `iss`: the AP's URL
- `agent`: the agent identifier (`aauth:local@domain`) this class token is bound to
- `class`: a single class string (opaque, AP-defined)
- `tenant`: OPTIONAL, scopes the class to a tenant for multi-tenant APs (semantics per existing auth-token `tenant` claim and OIDC.Enterprise)
- standard `iat` / `exp`

```json
{
  "iss":    "https://vendor.example",
  "agent":  "aauth:planner.7f3c@vendor.example",
  "class":  "planner",
  "tenant": "acme"
}
```

The AP issues one class token per class the agent is permitted to activate. An agent that belongs to multiple classes gets multiple class tokens.

### Presentation

The agent OPTIONALLY presents a class token when calling the PS token endpoint. Agents that don't use class don't present one — today's per-`agent_id` flow is unchanged.

When presenting, the agent picks the class token for whichever class it is operating as. The PS:

1. Verifies the class token signature against the AP's JWKS.
2. Verifies `class_token.agent` matches the agent identifier of the presenter.
3. Looks for a matching grant: `(AP, class)` or `(AP, class, tenant)`.

The PS never sees classes the agent didn't choose to activate — privacy beats the array-in-agent-token approach.

### Grant types

The PS already scopes everything to the user, so grants within a user's PS state come in three shapes:

- `agent_id` — per-instance grant (today's behavior)
- `(AP, class)` — class grant for per-user / per-tenant APs
- `(AP, class, tenant)` — class grant for multi-tenant APs

### What this avoids

- Agent token unchanged → no class/tenant exposure to resources in any access mode (two-, three-, four-party).
- No `classes` array → the PS only learns about the class the agent activates, not the agent's full taxonomy.
- No new claim semantics inside the agent token → fewer cross-token-type considerations.

### Net delta

- New artifact: AP-issued class token.
- New OPTIONAL parameter on the PS token endpoint to carry the class token.
- Class grant key at the PS is `(AP, class)` or `(AP, class, tenant)`, alongside the existing per-`agent_id` grant.
- Agent token: no change.

comments.body:
Field report from a personal AP serving multiple agent classes.

Picking up on your May-18 open question — *"it is not clear there is value to an individual to have a class of agents — would love to see use cases"* — here's one.

I run a personal AP (`ap.markmhendrickson.com`, conceptually) serving ~12 daemons under a single user (me). They split into a few natural classes:

- **read-only summarizers** (cotinga, morning-brief, anthus): pull from Neotoma + external feeds, write only summary entities back. Identical permission profile, identical risk surface.
- **write-back daemons** (turdus, tyto, neotoma-agent): write structured entities into Neotoma based on parsed inputs. Wider scope, higher consequence.
- **action daemons** (apus, formica, piculet, strix, monedula): take outbound actions (notifications, scheduled jobs, gmail triage, github harness). Each touches a different external resource.

Today, every daemon has its own agent_grant. When I add a new summarizer, I re-consent for the same shape I already approved three times. That's the friction class is designed to remove, and it absolutely shows up at n=12 personal agents under one user.

**Where I think the May-18 tenant-only stance breaks for personal APs:**

> *"when a new agent with a class calls the token endpoint, we don't know the user given the current token and API shapes — so we need to have to have the agent start a flow so we know which user is in context — which defeats having a preapproved class of agents. This indicates that a class should only apply to a tenant, not a user."*

The "we don't know which user is in context" problem is real for a *multi-tenant* AP. For a *personal* AP it's not — there's only one user. The AP knows. The PS knows. The bootstrap is already user-scoped.

One way to thread this:

- Define class grants as keyed on `(AP, class, scope_owner)` where `scope_owner` is *either* a tenant *or* a user.
- For multi-tenant APs, `scope_owner = tenant` (the protocol already has a tenant concept).
- For personal/single-user APs, `scope_owner = user_id`. This is fine because the AP-PS-user relationship is already established at bootstrap time — there's no "discover the user at token endpoint" step needed.
- Single-tenant APs (a SaaS that has only one customer) naturally map to either; pick one in deployment.

This avoids special-casing personal APs while not requiring the multi-tenant AP to know users.

**On the class-token-presented-only-to-PS reshape (your May-08 comment):**

I like this much more than the inline `class` claim. Three reasons specific to my topology:

1. Many of my daemons hit external resources (gmail, github, calendar) where the resource has no business knowing the daemon's class taxonomy. Class is genuinely PS-only routing metadata.
2. I want to be able to add a new class membership to an existing daemon without rotating its agent identity. The separate AP-issued class token makes this cheap (issue another class token, same agent identity) — much cleaner than re-minting an agent token with a different `classes` array.
3. Multi-class daemons are a real case for me: neotoma-agent is *both* a write-back daemon (for `interaction_type=feedback_shared`) *and* a summarizer (for derived entities). Per-class-token-per-class lets the daemon present the right class for the right operation rather than blanket-leaking its full taxonomy on every PS call.

**Cross-link to #23:** If sub-agents land as proposed there, sub-agents would NOT carry their own class tokens — they inherit authorization via parent's grant via `act.agent`. Class applies to top-level agents only. Worth calling out explicitly in either spec that class + sub-agent are orthogonal: top-level agents have classes, sub-agents have `act` chains, you don't combine them.

Happy to be a reference implementation for class + personal AP if helpful.

The split between instance identity and class-level consent seems necessary if agents are going to be usable in practice.

I would keep three concepts separate:

issues.title: Add sub-agents — single-level depth, parent-mediated authorization
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Background

Production AI agent platforms increasingly use sub-agent patterns: a parent agent (orchestrator) spawns short-lived child runtimes (workers, parallel tasks, tool-specific helpers) to do focused work. Today AAuth has no first-class way to express this:

- A sub-agent has no verifiable identity tied to its parent.
- A sub-agent has no authorization path that leverages the parent's grant.
- Operators have no way to attribute sub-agent activity to its spawning runtime.

The user has already consented to the parent. Sub-agents need to operate under that consent without per-spawn re-prompting, while still being identifiable for revocation and audit.

## Proposal

Sub-agents in three pieces.

### 1. Sub-agent identity

A sub-agent is an agent whose agent token contains a non-empty `act` claim referencing the parent.

```json
{
  "iss":   "https://vendor.example",
  "sub":   "aauth:planner.7f3c+search1@vendor.example",
  "cnf":   { "jwk": ... },
  "ps":    "https://ps.example",
  "act":   { "agent": "aauth:planner.7f3c@vendor.example" }
}
```

`act != ∅` in the agent token is the marker for sub-agent status. Verifiers check this; the local-part naming is for log readability only.

**Local-part naming convention (MUST):**

Sub-agent locals are `<parent-local>+<discriminator>`. Top-level locals MUST NOT contain `+`. Email convention (`dick+foo@gmail.com`). Verifiers MUST NOT parse the local part for protocol decisions — `act` is the source of truth. The convention is for operational readability.

### 2. Authorization flow

Sub-agents MUST NOT call the PS directly. The parent obtains auth tokens for them by calling the PS:

```
POST /auth-token at PS
  Signature-Key: parent's agent token       ← signs HTTP request
  Body:
    resource_token: sub-agent's resource token
    actor_token:    sub-agent's agent token
```

PS processes this as a normal authorization request from the parent:

- Verifies HTTP signature against the parent's `cnf.jwk`.
- Verifies `actor_token` (sub-agent's agent token) and that `act.agent` names the parent.
- Verifies `resource_token` is bound to the sub-agent's key.
- Looks up the parent's grant for the resource_token's scope. Same logic as a normal request from the parent.
- If grant covers it, issues an auth token bound to the sub-agent's key with `act.agent` = parent.

Same authorization logging as for the parent. If the user has already consented, the response is immediate. If not, the same interaction surfaces (for the parent) as for any new request.

The flow:

```
sub-agent → resource (gets resource token bound to sub-agent's key)
sub-agent → parent (passes resource token via IPC)
parent → PS (with sub-agent's resource token + agent token)
PS → parent (auth token bound to sub-agent's key)
parent → sub-agent (passes auth token via IPC)
sub-agent → resource (with auth token, signs with own key)
```

### 3. Single-level depth (MUST)

Sub-agents MUST NOT spawn their own sub-agents. Two parallel rules:

- PS MUST reject token requests from agents whose agent token has non-empty `act`.
- AP MUST reject spawn requests where the introducing party's agent token has non-empty `act`.

The chain is at most one level deep (top-level agent → sub-agent).

## Rationale

### Why single-level

Every production AI agent platform we surveyed caps sub-agent depth at 1:

- **Claude Code**: subagents cannot spawn other subagents. "Single-level structure prevents infinite nesting and keeps the execution hierarchy simple and manageable."
- **OpenAI Codex**: `agents.max_depth` defaults to 1. "Raising this value can turn broad delegation instructions into repeated fan-out, which increases token usage, latency, and local resource consumption."
- **Spring AI**: subagents cannot spawn their own subagents. The Task tool is explicitly excluded from subagent tool lists.

Where deeper structure exists in agent frameworks (LangGraph hierarchical teams, CrewAI hierarchical process), it's *design-time graph composition*, not runtime recursive spawning. The pattern is: orchestrator decomposes work, dispatches to workers, collects results. If a worker discovers more work, control returns to the orchestrator and it dispatches again.

For genuinely deep workflows, AAuth already has the right primitive: chained top-level agents (resource-acting-as-agent). Each chain level is a real principal with its own grant — no bubble-up authorization, no parent bottleneck.

### Why "sub-agents MUST NOT call PS"

- **Simpler PS state**: PS grants are keyed only on top-level agents. No sub-agent grant entries to track or revoke.
- **Parent retains control**: every authorization passes through the parent. Parent can refuse, attenuate, rate-limit, audit.
- **Natural revocation propagation**: revoke parent's grant → next sub-agent authorization fails. Existing auth tokens expire normally (≤1 hour).
- **No promotion path complexity**: a sub-agent can never accumulate independent authority. To become independent, you get a fresh parentless agent token from the AP — a different identity.

### Parent-mediated flow

The parent is the principal whose grant is checked; the sub-agent is the bearer of the resulting auth token. The PS treats the request like any normal authorization request from the parent — same grant lookup, same consent UX if needed, same logging. The novelty is just: bind the resulting auth token to the sub-agent's key, and put `act.agent` = parent in the chain.

This isn't token "cloning" — there's no prior auth token being propagated. It's a fresh authorization request, with a different binding target than usual.

### Why `+` convention as MUST

Operationally, log readability matters. Sub-agent identifiers like `aauth:planner.7f3c+search1@vendor.example` immediately tell an operator "sub-agent of `planner.7f3c`" without fetching the agent token. The email `+` convention (`dick+foo@gmail.com`) is universally understood. MUST-level (rather than SHOULD) ensures operators can rely on it ecosystem-wide. Verifiers still MUST NOT parse — `act` remains the cryptographic source of truth.

The cost is one breaking change to the local-part grammar (the existing example `aauth:cli+instance.1@tools.example` becomes `aauth:cli-instance.1@tools.example` or similar).

## Open questions

1. Are there real production use cases the orchestrator pattern (top-level + workers, depth 1) doesn't cover? If so, are they better served by chained top-level agents instead?
2. Should the AP's spawn protocol be normative or live in the bootstrap document (non-normative)? Lean toward bootstrap — the artifact (agent token shape) is what other parties verify; acquisition is a separate concern, parallel to top-level agent token bootstrap.


## References

- [Claude Code subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents)
- [OpenAI Codex Subagents](https://developers.openai.com/codex/subagents)
- [Spring AI Subagent Orchestration](https://spring.io/blog/2026/01/27/spring-ai-agentic-patterns-4-task-subagents/)
- [LangGraph Hierarchical Agent Teams](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/tutorials/multi_agent/hierarchical_agent_teams/)
- [Multi-Agent Systems and Subagents comparison: Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI](https://medium.com/@aristojeff/what-are-multi-agent-systems-and-subagents-a-comparison-of-codex-claude-code-and-gemini-cli-304376584f51)

comments.author: markmhendrickson
comments.body:
Field report from a personal swarm running this shape today.

I'm building Ateles, a personal agent fleet of ~12 named daemons (cotinga, cyphorhinus, anthus, apis, apus, turdus, tyto, formica, monedula, piculet, strix, neotoma-agent) coordinated by a single orchestrator (Onychomys). They share one user (me), write to one Neotoma instance, and each does a distinct narrow job — calendar prep, morning briefing, daily activity rollups, GitHub harness, etc. Today they all run as siblings with their own top-level AAuth identities and individual agent_grants. The act-chain sub-agent model in this proposal is closer to what the topology actually wants.

A few notes from running this in production for a few weeks:

**1. The single-level cap is right for my case, but the reason matters.**

I currently have zero need for depth >1. Onychomys is the only orchestrator; daemons don't spawn sub-workers, they run a single LLM turn and exit. So the Claude Code / Codex depth=1 precedent maps cleanly here. But the *reason* you cite — that deeper structure should fall back to chained top-level agents (resource-acting-as-agent) — is what makes this OK in practice. If I needed a daemon to fan out to its own workers, I'd want the workers to be chained top-level agents under the *user's* PS, not transitively-attenuated grandchildren under Onychomys's grant. That's a different cryptographic shape and the "use chained top-level agents instead" answer is the right one.

**2. Parent-mediated PS calls have an availability concern in my topology.**

Daemons are scheduled (cron-style) and run independently. Onychomys is event-driven and may be idle. If a daemon needs a fresh auth token at 05:30 and Onychomys isn't up, the daemon stalls.

Workarounds I can see:
- Pre-mint auth tokens at parent-spawn time with a TTL covering the expected daemon runtime (works for batch daemons, breaks for long-lived ones).
- Have the parent run as a persistent service whose only job is brokering PS calls (acceptable but adds a hot-path dependency).
- Allow the daemon to use a cached parent-issued auth token until expiry without re-mediation (this is roughly the current behavior since auth tokens are bearer-style within their lifetime — fine in practice).

I think the spec is already correct here (PS interaction is the parent's job, not the daemon's), but it'd be worth calling out in §Rationale that operators should pre-mint auth tokens with enough TTL to cover the daemon's actual runtime, or treat the parent as a persistent broker. The implicit assumption that the parent is always reachable when the sub-agent needs an auth token is the one production wrinkle I'd flag.

**3. On Nick Gamb's pushback (agents not principals, sub-agents get delegated tokens from a gateway).**

Both shapes solve the same problem (sub-agent gets scoped credentials without independent consent) but the trust-anchor placement is different:

- **Strata-style gateway**: gateway is the principal, holds the user's grant, mints attenuated tokens for sub-agents. The gateway is a real infrastructure component that has to exist and be trusted.
- **AAuth parent-mediated**: parent agent holds the grant, the PS mints sub-agent-key-bound auth tokens directly. No new infrastructure component, but the parent agent itself becomes load-bearing for trust.

For a personal swarm where the user already runs the parent, the AAuth shape has lower operational surface area — there's no gateway to deploy. For a multi-tenant SaaS where sub-agents fan out across customer boundaries, the gateway shape is probably right because you don't want any single tenant's parent agent to be inside the trust path for other tenants. I don't think these are mutually exclusive — the gateway pattern is naturally expressible as "the gateway is a top-level agent and sub-agents are chained from it," which the spec already supports. The parent-mediated path is the simpler default; gateway is what you build when you outgrow it.

**4. Local-part `+<discriminator>` convention in practice.**

I'd render my daemons as:
- `aauth:onychomys.7f3c+cotinga@ateles.markmhendrickson.com`
- `aauth:onychomys.7f3c+morning-brief@…`
- `aauth:onychomys.7f3c+neotoma-agent@…`

@christian-posta  @mcguinness 

Here is how I think these terms related to AAuth:

- platform: where the agent is running. web, mobile, desktop, self-hosted, workload. Self declared by agent at PS to help user understand where the agent is.
- surface: where the user is interacting with the agent. May be on the platform, common in web and mobile platform, but a web and mobile surface may be how the user is interacting with an agent running as on workload platform. Out of scope for AAuth.
- session: out of scope for AAuth
- mission: a context that grants may be given in. When an agent is granted access to a resource in the context of a mission, it does not have access outside of the mission.
- class: a mechanism for an agent to request access to any agent with the same class from the same AP. Once granted, any agent with that class has access to the same grant. If a class is presented in a mission, then any agent with the same class and a resource token with the same mission has access 

I worry that for large APs -- the class may be too broad -- there can be thousands of planner class agents across many users -- and the user does not want to do that -- so class may be better suited for APs scoped to an organization. 

building on #22

issues.title: R3: define r3_s256 as the hash of the exact served bytes, not RFC 8785 canonical JSON
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Summary
`draft-hardt-aauth-r3` computes `r3_s256` over the **RFC 8785 canonical JSON** serialization of the R3 document. Propose changing it to the SHA-256 of the **exact bytes the resource serves at `r3_uri`** (base64url, unpadded).

## Where the spec says canonical JSON
- **§Content Addressing**: "computed as the SHA-256 hash of the canonical JSON serialization ([@!RFC8785]) of the R3 document, base64url-encoded without padding."
- **§R3 Processing → AS Processing, step 3**: "Compute the SHA-256 hash of the fetched document using canonical JSON serialization ([@!RFC8785]) and compare it to `r3_s256`."

## Problem
Canonicalization is an extra, error-prone step on both sides: the resource serializes the document, and the AS/MM must re-serialize it **identically** (RFC 8785 — key ordering, number formatting, unicode normalization) before hashing. Any mismatch breaks verification. It buys nothing here, because the R3 document is **fetched as-is over HTTPS** — the verifier already holds the exact bytes.

## Proposal
Define `r3_s256` = `BASE64URL(SHA-256(served-bytes))`, where *served-bytes* are the exact response body the resource returns at `r3_uri`:
- The resource stringifies the document **once**, serves those bytes verbatim, and sets `r3_s256` to their hash.
- The AS/MM hash the **raw response body** they receive and compare. No canonicalization step.

## Rationale
- Simpler; removes a whole class of canonicalization-mismatch bugs.
- Content-addressing still holds: the hash identifies the exact served document.
- Matches the working reference implementation (`notes.aauth.dev`) and the deployed `person.hello.coop` behavior.

## Sections to update
- §Content Addressing — replace the RFC 8785 definition with the served-bytes hash.
- §AS Processing, step 3 — hash the raw fetched body.
- §R3 Document — keep "served over HTTPS, AS-signature-gated"; add that the resource MUST serve the exact bytes it hashed.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Resolved by #16 (merged). `r3_s256` is now defined as `BASE64URL(SHA-256(served-bytes))` — the SHA-256 of the exact bytes the resource serves at `r3_uri`, with no canonicalization step. See §Content Addressing; RFC 8785 is no longer referenced.

issues.title: R3: per-call escalation context — content-addressed proposal (params + recommended display sections), with hash-bound large payloads
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Summary
R3 `r3_conditional` already says the resource challenges a per-call operation "including the specific parameters from the agent's API request in the resource token," and the AS "evaluates those concrete parameters." But it doesn't define **how** to carry the parameters, **how the user sees the specific call** (the R3 `display` is per-document / per-class, not per-call), or what to do with **large payloads**. This proposes a concrete shape, reusing R3's content-addressing.

## Proposal: a per-call, content-addressed proposal document
For an escalate / `r3_conditional` operation, the resource builds a **per-call proposal document** — a per-instance R3 document with a fresh `r3_uri` / `r3_s256` (same content-addressing as the class doc; see #31 for the hashing fix) — holding:

- **`display`** — per-call Markdown for the PS to render to the user, with **recommended sections** (convention, not MUSTs, mirroring the `justification` "TODO: define recommended sections"): `## Action`, `## To` / `## Recipient`, `## Details`, `## Content` (excerpt), `## Irreversible`.
- **the specific parameters** — machine-readable, for the resource to bind and the AS to (optionally) evaluate. For large or sensitive payloads, store a **hash + short excerpt** instead of the bytes.

## Flow
1. Agent proposes the op (with parameters) at the authorization endpoint.
2. Resource stores the proposal and mints a resource_token referencing it (`r3_uri` / `r3_s256`). The token stays small — just the reference.
3. PS fetches the proposal (AS/PS-signature-gated), renders `display`, user approves → auth_token echoes `r3_uri` / `r3_s256`.
4. Agent retries the actual call → resource recovers the proposal from its own store and **enforces that the agent's actual parameters match what was approved** (and verifies `hash(payload)` for any re-presented large payload). "Approved: email mom" cannot become "email the CEO."

## Why this shape
- **Tokens stay small** — parameters are content-addressed, not inlined.
- **Large payloads never traverse the PS** — only a hash + excerpt do; the bytes go straight to the upstream at call time. Also a privacy lever (choose what the PS sees).
- **Binds approval to the exact proposed call** — the resource enforces an exact match.

## Open question
Whether the AS/PS should *machine-evaluate* the parameters (e.g., auto-deny payment > $X) or treat the proposal as display-for-human-consent only (v1). The parameters are present in the proposal either way, so machine policy can be added later without a format change.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Implemented in the R3 spec (§Per-Call Proposals, commit 1000d57 on `main`).

A per-call proposal is an R3 document scoped to a single invocation — same content-addressing as a class doc — carrying:
- `operations`: the single conditional op being invoked
- `parameters`: the concrete call parameters; large/sensitive values use a `{ s256, excerpt, media_type }` digest so payloads never traverse the PS
- `display.detail`: per-call Markdown with the recommended `## Action / ## To / ## Details / ## Content / ## Irreversible` sections

Flow: resource challenges the conditional call → builds + persists the proposal, references it (`r3_uri`/`r3_s256`) in the resource token → AS evaluates `parameters`, PS renders `display` → per-call auth token echoes the reference → on retry the resource binds the agent's actual parameters (and verifies digests) against the approved proposal, so an approval can't be replayed against a different call.

**Decisions taken:** (1) proposals are authored by the resource via the conditional challenge only — no proactive agent-declared parameters at the authorization endpoint (preserves the resource-declares property); (2) machine-evaluation of `parameters` (e.g. auto-deny payment > $X) is left as deployment policy, layerable without a format change.

Closing as implemented.

issues.title: interaction_endpoint: spec wrong about completion polling when interaction is hosted at a resource
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Issue

Section [§interaction-endpoint — Interaction Response](draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol.md) says:

> For `interaction` and `payment` types, the PS relays the interaction to the user and returns a deferred response (#deferred-responses). The agent polls until the user completes the interaction.

This implies the **PS's** deferred response terminates on user completion — i.e., the PS is the source of truth for "is the work done?"

But for the common case where the interaction URL points at a **resource** (e.g. a proxy's OAuth bootstrap page, a merchant's payment-confirmation page), the user actually completes the interaction at the resource, not at the PS. The PS only forwards the user there.

The agent ends up holding two pollUrls:
- one from the **resource** (the original `Location` on the resource's 202)
- one from the **PS** (the deferred response on the `interaction_endpoint` relay)

The spec doesn't say which one signals completion, or how the PS would learn that the resource has closed its pending.

## Suggested resolution

Clarify that for resource-hosted interaction URLs, the **resource's** pollUrl is authoritative for completion. The PS's deferred response should resolve when the user is engaged (e.g. has loaded the URL) or when the agent's optional `max_wait` window elapses — whichever comes first — and the agent then continues polling the resource pollUrl.

Equivalently: the PS could be required to relay the completion state from the resource, but that's more PS implementation burden (PS polls or subscribes to the resource).

## Related

Came up while building Ponte (a Cloudflare-Workers AAuth proxy) — OAuth bootstrap is a resource-hosted interaction, so the agent needs to know which pollUrl is authoritative.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Implemented (commit c39943f on `main`). §Interaction Response now distinguishes PS-hosted vs resource-hosted interaction URLs. For the resource-hosted case (the common relayed one), **the resource's original `Location` is authoritative for completion**; the PS relay deferred response reports only engagement via `status: "interacting"` and resolves on engagement, an optional agent-supplied `max_wait` window, or when the PS can make no further progress. Added the OPTIONAL `max_wait` interaction request parameter. Closing.

issues.title: interaction_endpoint: define error code for 'PS cannot perform the interaction'
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Two pieces — both around `interaction_endpoint`

### 1. Define the agent's "try PS first" flow

The spec today ([§requirement-responses:895](draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol.md#L895)) says when an agent receives `202 + AAuth-Requirement: requirement=interaction; url=…`, it directs the user to that URL itself. There's no step where the agent first asks the PS to drive the interaction.

We should specify that **the agent SHOULD POST the interaction to the PS's `interaction_endpoint` before driving the URL itself**, so the PS can use any direct user-reach channels it has (live web session, registered mobile push). The agent only drives the URL directly when the PS reports it cannot.

Flow becomes:
1. Agent receives `202 + AAuth-Requirement: requirement=interaction; url=…; code=…` from a resource (or AS or PS).
2. Agent POSTs `{type: "interaction", url, code, …}` to PS's `interaction_endpoint`.
3. PS attempts to reach the user via its channels.
4. PS returns `202 + Location:` (deferred poll) on success, OR the new error below on failure.
5. On the error, agent drives the URL directly (browser-open, QR, etc.).

### 2. Define the error for "PS cannot perform the interaction"

The existing `interaction_required` error ([§polling-error-codes:2016](draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol.md#L2016)) doesn't fit: it means "interaction is needed but **no party** can drive it" — a terminal two-sided failure. Our case is one-sided: the agent **can** drive the interaction, it just preferred the PS try first.

Proposed new error:

| code | HTTP | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `interaction_unavailable` | 4xx (TBD) | The PS has no channel available to reach the user for this interaction. The agent should fall back to driving the URL directly. |

Name and exact HTTP status open for discussion. Some 4xx options: `400`, `409 Conflict`, `422 Unprocessable Entity`, `424 Failed Dependency`. (5xx feels wrong since it's not a server fault — it's expected protocol state.)

`interaction_required` keeps its existing meaning unchanged.

## Related

- [#33](https://github.com/dickhardt/AAuth/issues/33) — interaction_endpoint completion-polling clarification (same endpoint, different ambiguity)
- [hellocoop/Wallet#4055](https://github.com/hellocoop/Wallet/issues/4055) — Wallet implementation of `interaction_endpoint`, which needs both the new flow and the new error code
- Driver: Ponte's agent (praca) needs this to do PS-first interaction-driving with graceful fallback to local browser open / QR

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Implemented (commit 5ace301 on `main`).

**Try-PS-first flow** (§Requirement Responses → Relaying Through the Person Server): an agent with a PS SHOULD relay the interaction to the PS's `interaction_endpoint` before driving the URL itself; it falls back to browser/QR/display only when it has no PS or the PS declines.

**New error** `interaction_unavailable` (**424 Failed Dependency**), defined in §Interaction Endpoint Errors: the PS has no channel to relay this specific interaction. Non-terminal — the agent falls back to driving the URL. Explicitly distinguished from the terminal `user_unreachable` (no party can reach the user). Closing.

issues.title: Capabilities: token endpoint body parameter, not header (and mission-less use)
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Summary

`capabilities` belongs in the **token request body**, not in a header. Headers are only used when there is a conflict with a pre-existing API; for the PS token endpoint, the body is the right place. §12.1's exclusion of `AAuth-Capabilities` on PS endpoints stands — that header is for resource calls.

Hellō's behavior is correct; the spec just needs to catch up and list `capabilities` as a standard token endpoint parameter alongside `resource_token`, `justification`, etc.

## Mission interaction

When a request is part of a mission, the agent does not need to send `capabilities` again — the PS already has them from the approval flow. But the agent **MAY** include them if it wants to, or if they have changed since approval.

## Proposed change

- Add `capabilities` to the PS token endpoint request parameter list (body), alongside `resource_token`, `justification`, etc.
- Note that within a mission, `capabilities` is optional; if omitted, the PS uses the values captured at approval; if present, it overrides/refreshes for this request.
- Keep §12.1's rule that `AAuth-Capabilities` (the header form) is for resource calls only, not PS endpoints.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Implemented (commit 51f139d on `main`). Added `capabilities` as a PS **token endpoint request-body** parameter — the body equivalent of `AAuth-Capabilities`, which §AAuth-Capabilities still excludes from PS endpoints. Without a mission it's how the PS learns capabilities; within a mission it's OPTIONAL (omitted → PS uses approval-time values; present → refreshes for this request). Closing.

issues.title: Polling errors: distinguish user_unreachable (terminal) from interaction_required (non-terminal)
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Summary

`interaction_required` and `user_unreachable` are two distinct conditions and should be modeled distinctly in the spec's polling/terminal error table.

## The two conditions

- **`interaction_required`** — returned in a `202`, **non-terminal**. The PS needs the agent to direct the user somewhere (URL + code). Polling continues.
- **`user_unreachable`** — **terminal error**. The PS has no channel to the user and the agent did not declare interaction capability, so there is no way to reach the user at all.

## State of the spec

Hellō's current behavior — returning `user_unreachable` on the missing-capabilities case — is correct. What is missing is `user_unreachable` itself in the spec's polling/terminal error table.

## Proposed change (target: -02)

Add `user_unreachable` to the polling/terminal error table as a terminal error, with the trigger condition "PS has no channel to the user and the agent did not declare interaction capability." Keep `interaction_required` as the non-terminal 202 path.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Implemented (commit 5ace301 on `main`). The spec's existing `interaction_required` (403) terminal error *was* this condition — renamed to `user_unreachable` in the Token Endpoint Error Codes table, clarified as **terminal** (PS has no channel AND agent didn't declare the `interaction` capability). The non-terminal 'user action needed' case keeps using a `202` with `requirement=interaction`. Closing.

Two related parameters surfaced by Hellō's implementation:

### `prompt` — add to the spec

`prompt` should be in the spec. It is OIDC vocabulary, and AAuth already reuses OIDC for `login_hint`, `tenant`, and `domain_hint`. Add it to §7.1.3 in -02 with the OIDC values:

- `none`
- `login`
- `consent`
- `select_account`

### `provider_hint` — stays Hellō-specific

`provider_hint` is a Hellō extension. It steers between consumer providers (email, Google, etc.) and does not generalize across PSes. Not adding to the spec.

## Proposed change (target: -02)

- §7.1.3: add `prompt` with the four OIDC values above, referencing OIDC Core 1.0 §3.1.2.1.
- No spec change for `provider_hint`; document it as a Hellō-specific extension if/where appropriate (out of band).

issues.title: Add AAuth-Requirement: requirement=agent-token for identity-only access
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Problem

When a resource needs only an agent token (Level 1 / identity access mode — no user auth token), there's no clean way for it to signal that on a `401`:

- `Accept-Signature` with `sigkey=uri` is too broad — it accepts any URI-identified key (jwks_uri or jwt scheme), not specifically an AAuth agent token (`typ: aa-agent+jwt`).
- `Signature-Error` is for signature verification failures, not for "you're not presenting the right kind of token."
- `AAuth-Requirement` has no value covering this case today — `auth-token` is for the user-identity path.

## Proposal

Add a new `AAuth-Requirement` value:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
AAuth-Requirement: requirement=agent-token
```

Symmetric with `requirement=auth-token`. The header carries no additional parameters — the agent already holds its agent token; the resource is just signaling that it must be presented via `Signature-Key: sig=jwt;jwt=…`.

## Resulting 401 layering

| Condition | Response |
|---|---|
| No signature presented | `401` + `Signature-Error: error=invalid_signature` (+ optionally `Accept-Signature` with `sigkey`) |
| Signature present, resource wants an AAuth agent token | `401` + `AAuth-Requirement: requirement=agent-token` |
| Agent identified, needs user auth/consent | `401` + `AAuth-Requirement: requirement=auth-token; resource-token="…"` |
| Agent identified, denied by policy | `403` |

## Naming

Considered `requirement=identity` (concept-level, parallel to `interaction`). Rejected because AAuth has exactly two token types — agent token and auth token — and `agent-token` is symmetric with the existing `auth-token` value, naming exactly the artifact the resource needs.

## Spec edits

1. New row in the Requirement Values table (currently at line 1823 of `draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol.md`):
   `| agent-token | 401 | Agent token required for resource identification | Y | | |`
2. Update the identity / agent-only access mode section to describe the `requirement=agent-token` challenge as the way a resource asks for an agent token when none was presented. (No standalone subsection needed — this lives in the identity-level description.)
3. Update §Error Responses (around line 1996) to clarify the split: `Signature-Error` for missing/malformed signatures, `AAuth-Requirement` for the resource asking for a specific AAuth token type.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: Implemented (commit 51f139d on `main`). Added `requirement=agent-token` (401) with a new §Agent Token Required and an AAuth Requirement Value Registry entry. It signals the resource specifically requires an AAuth agent token (`typ: aa-agent+jwt`) — distinct from `auth-token` (no PS/AS involved) and more specific than an `Accept-Signature` challenge, which would accept any URI-identified key. The agent presents its agent token via `Signature-Key: sig=jwt;jwt=…`. Closing.

issues.title: Call chaining across domains: directed sub re-expression and iss:sub ↔ iss:sub mapping
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Background

In call chaining (§Call Chaining / §Multi-Hop), a resource acts as an agent to access a downstream resource. The spec explicitly **preserves the `act` delegation chain** across the hop (Upstream Token Verification step 4: "nesting the upstream token's `act` claim inside a new `act` object… preserves the complete delegation chain") and uses the upstream `iss` for routing/trust. But it is **silent on `sub`** across a domain boundary.

## The gap

`sub` in AAuth is **directed and namespaced by issuer**:
- "the same `sub` value from a different PS is a different subject" (§PS-asserted access)
- the PS provides "a directed `sub` identifier for the resource" (§AS Response, `requirement=claims`)

When chaining crosses domains, the downstream auth token is issued by a **different `iss`** and should carry a **different directed `sub`** for the **same** user. The chaining narrative never states this, nor how the downstream issuer obtains the right `sub`. A reader is left to infer it from the directed-`sub` rules in other sections.

Surfaced during review of #23 (sub-agents), via this worked example: across `booking@domain1 → payments@domain2`, the `act` chain carries through (agent identifiers are global) but `sub` must be re-expressed as domain-2's directed identifier for the same user.

## What needs discussion

1. **State the behavior**: across a domain boundary the downstream token carries a new `iss` (the downstream issuer) and a new directed `sub` for the same user, while the `act` chain is preserved.

2. **The mapping problem** — how does one `(iss, sub)` map to another `(iss, sub)` for the same human?
   - The PS is the cross-domain identity anchor (it knows `alice@domain1 ≡ alice@domain2`). By what mechanism does it perform/assert the mapping?
   - **Governed path** (mission present): the PS brokers both hops and can supply the directed `sub` for the downstream resource via the claims flow. Spell this out.
   - **Ungoverned four-party path** (no mission, `iss` is an AS): there is no PS in the loop — the downstream AS receives only the `upstream_token` + the intermediary's agent token. How does it determine the user's directed `sub` in its own domain? Does it get a user `sub` at all, or only the agent `act` chain (i.e., agent-identity access with no user subject)?

3. **Privacy**: directed/pairwise `sub` means resources cannot correlate the user across domains. Confirm this property holds through chains and that nothing in the upstream token leaks a correlatable identifier downstream.

4. **Should the upstream `sub` ever travel downstream at all**, or only the downstream-issuer-asserted directed `sub`?

## Related
- #23 (sub-agents) — where this surfaced.

issues.title: Add access_mode to aauth-resource.json to signal the agent flow
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Summary

Add a single scalar field `access_mode` to `/.well-known/aauth-resource.json` that tells an agent which credential flow the resource expects. Three values cover the deployment shapes and map directly onto the three migration stories from existing auth patterns. Runtime `401` + `AAuth-Requirement` remains authoritative; the declaration is advisory.

## Motivation

Today an agent must either:

1. Try-and-401: call the resource, react to challenges. Works, but costs a round-trip on every first call to a new endpoint.
2. Read `aauth-resource.json` and infer modes from the presence/absence of fields (e.g., `authorization_endpoint`, `scope_descriptions`). Unstated; brittle.

A single declarative field lets a smart agent plan upfront — pick the right wire format on the first call, pre-fetch any needed tokens, and pre-filter resources it can't satisfy (e.g., a PS-less agent skipping resources that require an auth token).

It also gives resource adopters a clean answer to "what do I declare?" by mapping each AAuth migration story to one value:

- API-key resource → `agent-token`
- OAuth-scoped resource → `aauth-access-token`
- New / dynamic auth (PS-asserted or federated) → `auth-token`
- Greenfield with R3 → `auth-token` plus vocabularies

## Proposed change

### New field

```json
{
  "issuer": "https://resource.example",
  "jwks_uri": "https://resource.example/.well-known/jwks.json",
  "access_mode": "auth-token"
}
```

`access_mode` (OPTIONAL): one of `agent-token`, `aauth-access-token`, `auth-token`. Default: `agent-token`.

### Agent behavior per value

| `access_mode` | What the agent does |
|---------------|---------------------|
| `agent-token` | Sign with agent token (`Signature-Key:`), call. No further authorization. |
| `aauth-access-token` | Go through the resource's `authorization_endpoint` (or trigger a 401), complete interaction/consent at the resource, receive an opaque token in `AAuth-Access:`, present it in `Authorization: AAuth ...` plus signature on subsequent calls. |
| `auth-token` | Get a resource token from `authorization_endpoint` or 401, send to the agent's PS, receive an auth token, sign with it. Whether the PS asserts identity directly (three-party) or federates with the resource's AS (four-party) is invisible to the agent. |

### Authority and mixing

- The declaration is advisory. The resource MAY return any `AAuth-Requirement` at runtime regardless of declared mode (e.g., to require auth-token on a specific protected endpoint even when the resource is declared `agent-token`).
- Mixed resources (e.g., a primarily OAuth-wrapped resource with some public endpoints) declare their primary mode; agents discover exceptions via 401.
- 401 + `AAuth-Requirement` is the contract; `access_mode` is the planning hint.

### Capability pre-filtering

Agents MAY use `access_mode` to skip resources their setup cannot satisfy:

- PS-less agent (no `ps` claim in agent token) → can use `agent-token` and `aauth-access-token` resources; SHOULD skip `auth-token` resources.
- PS-bearing agent → can use any mode.

### Migration stories

The "Resource Adoption Path" section should be rewritten around the three migration paths plus greenfield:

1. **API key → `agent-token`.** Replace the API-key check with HTTP Message Signature verification. Agent identity becomes cryptographically verifiable; no other infrastructure changes.
2. **OAuth scopes → `aauth-access-token`.** Wrap the existing OAuth access token in `AAuth-Access:`. Existing OAuth infrastructure stays; signature binding is added; the agent goes through `authorization_endpoint` for consent.
3. **Dynamic / per-call auth → `auth-token`.** Issue resource tokens at `authorization_endpoint` or 401. The agent's PS exchanges them for auth tokens. Three-party or federated; the agent doesn't need to know which.
4. **Greenfield with R3.** Same as `auth-token` plus publishing vocabularies and R3 documents (see [draft-hardt-aauth-r3](./draft-hardt-aauth-r3.md)).

## Why `access_mode` is scalar (not an array)

In practice, each resource has a primary mode. Mixed cases (a resource that genuinely supports two modes at different endpoints) are handled by runtime 401 escalation without needing to enumerate both modes upfront. The capability pre-filter works at "can I use this resource at all" granularity, which is what scalar declaration captures.

## Why three values (not four)

The original spec defines four access modes: identity, resource-managed (two-party), PS-asserted (three-party), federated (four-party). From the **agent's** perspective, three-party and four-party are the same code path — the agent always sends the resource token to its own PS and gets back an auth token. The PS-internal federation to a resource AS is invisible to the agent. So collapsing both into `auth-token` accurately names what the agent has to do.

The four-party-vs-three-party distinction is a deployment property of the resource (does it have its own AS?) and remains visible in the resource token's `aud`, in the resource's AS metadata (if any), and in audit logs. It just doesn't need to surface in `access_mode`.

## Why not per-operation declarations in OpenAPI

Earlier discussion explored adding AAuth-aware security schemes to OpenAPI / MCP / other vocabularies. Conclusions:

- OpenAPI's `securitySchemes` doesn't have a native fit for HTTP Message Signatures in `Signature-Key:` (only `type: apiKey` works as a shim, which mis-describes the credential).
- IANA's HTTP Authentication Scheme Registry is specifically for `Authorization:` schemes — fine for the opaque `AAuth` access token, doesn't cover `Signature-Key:` modes.
- Most resources are uniformly one mode; per-op declarations would be noise.
- For the rare mixed-mode resource, per-op overrides in the vocabulary remain a deferred optimization for least-privilege batching.

Per-op annotations stay on the table for R3 v2 or future work; they're not needed for v1.

## Spec changes required

1. Add `access_mode` field to "Resource Metadata" section (`/.well-known/aauth-resource.json`).
2. Add normative text: declaration is advisory; runtime 401 is authoritative.
3. Add agent guidance on using `access_mode` for capability pre-filtering.
4. Rewrite "Resource Adoption Path" around the three migration stories plus greenfield.
5. Update "Adoption Matrix" to reference `access_mode` values.

## Open questions

- Field name: `access_mode` vs `mode` vs `auth_mode`. Lean `access_mode` to align with existing "resource access modes" terminology.
- Default behavior when omitted: proposed `agent-token`. Alternative is "no default; explicit declaration required." Default is preferred because it keeps the minimum-viable resource trivial to publish (`issuer` + `jwks_uri` only) while staying correct via runtime 401.

comments.body: Implemented on `main` for -02. `access_mode` added to resource metadata (`agent-token` / `aauth-access-token` / `auth-token`, default `agent-token`, advisory with runtime `AAuth-Requirement` authoritative, PS-less capability pre-filtering). Also added the §Drop-In Replacement for API Keys and OAuth framing and a §Consuming a Resource End to End walkthrough (metadata discovery via access_mode + R3 vocabulary, learn-the-API, bring the user in per mode), noted in Bootstrapping that resources SHOULD publish access_mode + an R3 vocabulary, ordered the resource-access challenge sections weakest-to-strongest, and relaxed `jwks_uri` to be required only when the resource issues resource tokens or makes signed calls. Closing.
