issues.title: Sub-agents (Section 11) — cross-walk to OWASP AISVS C9.2.7 worst-case chain rule + CSA NHI 6-property chain audit schema
issues.author: Mayur021
issues.body:
## Background

  Congratulations on -02. Section 11 (Sub-Agents) introduces a clean per-sub-agent identity primitive — separate signing key, `parent_agent` claim, individual revocability via `subagent_token`. This addresses the WHO axis of composed agent delegation cleanly.

  There are two adjacent standards-track surfaces worth referencing where the AAuth-02 sub-agents work intersects.

  ## Cross-walk 1 — OWASP AISVS C9.2.7

  [OWASP AISVS C9.2.7](https://github.com/OWASP/AISVS/blob/main/research/chapters/C09-Orchestration-and-Agents/C09-02-High-Impact-Action-Approval.md) (Proposed for 1.01, merged 2026-05-27) — the worst-case action class chain rule:

  > "Verify that... before a multi-step agent chain begins execution, the gate is set by the least-reversible, highest-blast-radius action the chain
   can reach (worst-case governs)."

  Where AAuth-02 §11.3 governs WHO can act (parent mediates sub-agent authorization), AISVS C9.2.7 governs WHAT classes of action are reachable across the composed chain. The two layers compose: AAuth handles the identity delegation; AISVS handles the action-class authority across composed steps. A sub-agent's authorized action class should also bind to the worst-case class reachable by the parent's tool set, not just to the sub-agent's individual authorization scope.

  ## Cross-walk 2 — CSA NHI 6-property chain audit schema

  **CSA NHI chain-level audit schema (under IAM WG peer review, joint with Mallikarjunarao Sunke)** — six-property schema:

  1. Chain id
  2. Declared worst-case action class at chain start
  3. Gate decision + justification per step
  4. Per-step API record
  5. Originating principal
  6. Immutability of originating principal

  The AAuth-02 mission log (Section 8.3) maps to property 4 (per-step API record) and the `parent_agent` claim maps to property 5 (originating
  principal). The remaining properties (chain-id, declared worst-case class, immutability cryptographic property) would complement AAuth-02's audit posture.

  ## Specific suggestion

  A future revision could reference AISVS C9.2.7 + CSA NHI 6-property audit schema in §11 (Sub-Agents) or §8 (Mission) to ground the action-class +
  audit-schema layers that compose with AAuth-02's identity delegation work.

  ## References

  - OWASP AISVS C9.2.6 + C9.2.7: [OWASP/AISVS#822](https://github.com/OWASP/AISVS/pull/822) (merged main 2026-05-27)
  - CSA NHI 6-property schema: under CSA Identity & Access Management Working Group peer review
  - [PieterKas/agent2agent-auth-framework#114](https://github.com/PieterKas/agent2agent-auth-framework/issues/114) (reversibility-graded CIBA step-up)

  ---

  (Author: Mayur Agnihotri — OWASP AISVS Contributor + CSA IAM WG Reviewer + filed PieterKas#114)

issues.title: Align aauth-resource.json fields with RFC 9728 (OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata)
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Background

RFC 9728 defines [OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9728) with an IANA registry of standard field names. Comparing AAuth's current well-known metadata files against RFC 9728 and across the four AAuth server roles reveals several naming inconsistencies.

## Decision: `issuer` not `resource`

RFC 9728 uses `resource` as the primary identifier. AAuth standardizes on `issuer` across all dwk files.

The concrete reason: a verifier receiving a `Signature-Key` header with a `dwk` claim or parameter needs to fetch `{iss}/.well-known/{dwk}` and extract two things — `issuer` (to confirm the document belongs to the claimed signer) and `jwks_uri` (to retrieve the signing keys). With `issuer` present in every dwk file, the verifier can perform this check uniformly without knowing whether the URL resolves to an agent provider, resource, person server, or access server. Without a consistent `issuer` field, a generic Signature-Key verifier would need role-specific parsing to extract the signer identity and key location. See also: the Signature-Key spec should define `issuer` as a SHOULD field in the metadata document schema (filed separately in draft-hardt-httpbis-signature-key).

Document this intentional divergence from RFC 9728.

## Decision: `name` across all dwk files

AAuth's design principle is uniform dwk processing — every well-known file has the same base shape. A role-specific name field (`client_name`, `resource_name`, `agent_name`) carries wrong conceptual baggage and creates unnecessary asymmetry. Each dwk file is already namespaced by its filename, so there is no ambiguity.

**Change:** use `name` (OPTIONAL) in all four well-known metadata files, replacing `client_name` in `aauth-agent.json` and the previously proposed `resource_name` in `aauth-resource.json`.

This intentionally diverges from RFC 9728's `resource_name` — document the divergence in the spec.

## Decision: consistent unprefixed URI fields

RFC 9728 uses prefixed names (`resource_tos_uri`, `resource_policy_uri`, `resource_documentation`). `aauth-agent.json` already uses unprefixed `tos_uri` and `policy_uri`. For consistency across all dwk files, use the unprefixed forms everywhere:

- `tos_uri` (not `resource_tos_uri`)
- `policy_uri` (not `resource_policy_uri`)
- `documentation_uri` (not `resource_documentation` — URL with developer/usage information)

## Common fields for all dwk files

These OPTIONAL fields should appear consistently across `aauth-agent.json`, `aauth-resource.json`, `aauth-person.json`, and `aauth-access.json`. Consider defining them once in a "Common Metadata Fields" section and referencing it from each per-role section, rather than repeating the definitions four times.

| Field | agent | resource | PS | AS |
|-------|-------|----------|----|----|
| `issuer` | ✓ REQUIRED | ✓ REQUIRED | ✓ REQUIRED | ✓ REQUIRED |
| `jwks_uri` | ✓ REQUIRED | ✓ REQUIRED (conditional) | ✓ REQUIRED | ✓ REQUIRED |
| `name` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `description` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `logo_uri` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `logo_dark_uri` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `tos_uri` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `policy_uri` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `documentation_uri` | ✗ missing | ✓ | ✗ missing | ✗ missing |

## `scope_descriptions` (keep as-is)

AAuth's `scope_descriptions` maps scope values to Markdown strings for consent display. This is intentionally different from RFC 9728's `scopes_supported` (an array). No change.

issues.title: act chain: use `agent` instead of `sub` within `act` claims
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Background

The current spec uses RFC 8693's `act` claim to record delegation chains in auth tokens, with `sub` as the identifier field inside each `act` node:

```json
{
  "act": { "sub": "aauth:booking@booking.example",
           "act": { "sub": "aauth:asst@agent.example" } }
}
```

## Problem with `sub`

1. **Ambiguity** — `sub` is a generic JWT term ("subject") that could hold any kind of identifier. Nothing in the field name tells the reader this is an AAuth agent identifier.
2. **Name collision confusion** — the outer JWT already has its own `sub` (the user). Readers must track two semantically different `sub` fields simultaneously.
3. **The chain is AAuth-specific anyway** — RFC 8693 defines the nesting structure of `act`, but AAuth already uses `aauth:` URIs as the values, which are not standard `sub` values. Using a generic field name obscures what the value actually represents.

## Proposed change

Replace `sub` with `agent` inside every `act` node:

```json
{
  "act": { "agent": "aauth:booking@booking.example",
           "act": { "agent": "aauth:asst@agent.example" } }
}
```

This reads cleanly: every node in the chain is unambiguously an AAuth agent identifier in `aauth:` URI form. The field name is consistent whether the hop is a sub-agent or a call-chain intermediary — both place an `aauth:` URI in `act.agent`.

## Trade-off

This diverges from RFC 8693's `act.sub` convention, which implementors coming from Token Exchange might expect. However, since the values are `aauth:` URIs (already non-standard `sub` values), anything consuming this chain is AAuth-specific code regardless. The adaptation cost is low, especially while sub-agents are new and not yet widely implemented.

## Scope of change

- Auth token `act` claim definition (#auth-tokens)
- Auth token verification steps (check `act.agent` not `act.sub`)
- Call chaining section: PS construction of nested `act` claim
- Sub-agents section: parent-mediated auth token examples
- The three composite examples (just chaining, just a sub-agent, sub-agent + chain)
- IANA JWT Claims registration note (document intentional divergence from RFC 8693)

issues.title: Extension proposal: DID-binding profile for Person Servers (aka 'Avatar')
issues.author: eatplaysleep
issues.body:
# Extension proposal: DID-binding profile for Person Servers (Avatar)

**Summary:** Dasith Wijesiriwardena's ["The Errand"](https://dasith.me/2026/06/10/the-errand-agentic-delegation/) names two edges of agentic delegation that AAuth doesn't yet close: the bilateral setup a Person Server still needs with every new resource (Dad gets linked as trusted contact "the first time the family deals with the chain"), and the open question of delegation containment — whether a sub-agent actually stayed inside what its parent was authorized to do, as opposed to the protocol merely being able to show that a handoff took place. This issue proposes **Avatar**: a DID-binding profile for Person Servers that closes both, without breaking changes to the existing spec.

---

## The gap, in Errand terms

AAuth gives Sam (the Agent) a precise, per-instance cryptographic identity — that's the protocol's central win. It doesn't give Dad (the Person Server) the same thing. Dad is reachable at a URL, but a URL isn't a portable identity, which shows up as two concrete problems:

- **First-time setup, every time.** Each new resource chain has to independently establish that this Dad really speaks for this Mom before trusting him — the exact bilateral setup AAuth's agent-side identity was built to avoid.  
- **No containment proof.** When Sam delegates to his little brother, the protocol can show the handoff happened, but not that the brother stayed inside what Sam was actually authorized to do. Call chaining proves the chain; it doesn't bound it.

Both stem from the same root cause: no portable, independently verifiable identity root for the *human*, only for the agent.

## The proposal

Three additive pieces, all fitting within existing AAuth extension points:

1. **DID-anchored PS discovery** — a `did` claim in `/.well-known/aauth-person.json`, resolvable to a DID document whose `aauth-person` service endpoint confirms the PS URL. No bilateral setup required; PS URL can change while the DID stays stable.  
     
2. **Avatar agent token** — an agent token with `avatar: true` and `ps_did` claims indicating the agent *is* the person's primary agent, with its identity root anchored to the human's DID rather than an ephemeral keypair.  
     
3. **Delegation assertion** — a signed JWT from an Avatar agent vouching for a sub-agent's identity and constraining its authority, scoped to a Mission. Allows agent-to-agent delegation without requiring a new PS consent interaction per sub-agent call.

All three use existing AAuth JWT signing profiles and token structures. The delegation assertion is the only net-new artifact.

## Full write-up

Detailed proposal with JSON examples, open questions, and explicit non-goals (this is not a competing protocol; it's not DID maximalism):

[Avatar: A DID-Binding Profile for AAuth Person Servers](https://gist.github.com/eatplaysleep/419ea3f313df2e8ab873aa2123857c87)

## Open questions I'd like community input on

- Should the profile constrain allowed DID methods, or stay method-agnostic? (`did:web` has adoption advantages; `did:key` has stronger self-sovereignty guarantees)  
- Should delegation chains be depth-bounded before a PS interaction is required?  
- How does this interact with the federated four-party access mode in enterprise deployments where the org operates both the DID and the PS?

Happy to iterate on any of this — particularly the delegation JWT structure, which I know touches the scope-vs-intent tension in the current spec.

---

comments.body: @eatplaysleep how do you think this fits in with x401?  https://x401.proof.com/spec/latest/ -- I have a call queued up with @csuwildcat Daniel Buchner to discuss?

comments.author: eatplaysleep
comments.body:
Hey @dickhardt -- appreciate your patience on my incredibly delayed reply. I would be very curious about your discussion with @csuwildcat! 

x401 is a no-brainer to me and, honestly, I am kind of amazed it took this long to come about! 

My initial thought is that it is complementary to AAuth and Avatar, not competing. 
- x401 gates the resource → `prove X to get in`
- AAuth authorizes the agent → `who are you acting for, what can you do?` 
- Avatar is the human identity root that lets both point at the same thing instead of each building their own trust setup 
 
The Agent Identifier field already leaves the door open for a DID scheme.

I think the x401 open questions regarding fully autonomous delegation and agent authentication look like the natural landing spot for AAuth (and Avatar). 

What are your thoughts on x401 and AAuth?

issues.title: Mission-log completeness under agent–PS partition: a gap §14.16 and §12.7.4.1 don't close
issues.author: ZeeshanKhanSA
issues.body:
v08's §14.16 (non-repudiation after key rotation) and §12.7.4.1 (freshness and replay) close the request-level cases well: archive-at-verification preserves "key K signed request R at time T," and the `created`-window replay cache rejects duplicate request tuples. Both operate on the signed HTTP request at the resource/verifier. I want to surface a residual case they don't reach, at the mission-governance layer, when the agent is partitioned from its PS — a long-running, intermittent, or `workload`/`self-hosted` (§16.9) agent acting across a network gap.

The setup: §7.5.2 keeps audit fire-and-forget ("the agent SHOULD NOT block on the response"), and `approved_tools` (§7.4, §8.2) let the agent act locally without reaching the PS per action. §8.3 keeps the asymmetry — the mission description is `s256`-immutable, but the mission log is a PS-maintained ordered record with no expected-sequence integrity of its own. Two cases follow:

1. **Suppression / tail-truncation**. A partitioned agent performs `approved_tools` actions and never emits the corresponding audit records. §14.16's archive-at-verification doesn't help here: the agent made no request to any verifier while disconnected, so there's nothing to archive. The PS can't distinguish "agent did nothing during the gap" from "agent acted and didn't report it," because the log has no issued sequence the agent must account for. (This is the tail-truncation @jagmarques flagged in #3 — an external witness catches mid-log edits but not a silently short tail.)
2. **Stale-mission replay**. Distinct from §12.7.4.1's request replay. The agent re-presents an earlier validly-signed mission state as current after the surrounding context moved on — e.g. the mission was revoked per §8.5/§12.6 during the partition. `s256` still verifies (the mission is immutable by design), and §12.7.4.1's cache is scoped to the `created` window (default 60s) and to duplicate request tuples, so neither signals that the mission state is stale at the multi-hour timescale of a partition.

The distinction I'd want explicit: §14.16 gives durable evidence of requests that were made and verified; §12.7.4.1 bounds replay of a single signed request within its window. Neither makes a gap in what the agent should have logged, or a replayed-stale mission state, detectable after reconnection. Closing those needs something at the agent↔PS contract level — a per-mission monotonic counter or pre-issued `jti`/nonce range the PS issues and the agent must consume in order, so a missing index is detectable rather than invisible. That's wire surface (what the PS hands the agent), not PS storage internals — which is why I think it's protocol-shaped rather than the kind of PS-implementation detail that closed PR #10.

So, concretely: (a) Is offline/deferred governance in scope — may an agent perform `approved_tools` actions while it can't reach the PS, or is the model strictly online? (b) If deferred governance is in scope, does the expected-sequence contract belong in the §8.5 companion spec for mission state transitions, or is mission-log completeness considered out of protocol scope entirely (as PR #10's chaining was)? Genuinely unsure where the line sits, which is why I'm asking. Happy to write the partition cases up as concrete sequences.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed analysis — the distinction between request-level integrity (§14.16, §12.7.4.1) and mission-log completeness is drawn precisely, and the two cases are worth addressing directly.

**On (a): offline deferred governance is in scope.** `approved_tools` is explicitly designed for agents that act without per-action PS contact — headless workloads, intermittently-connected agents, and self-hosted deployments are first-class use cases. An agent performing approved tools while partitioned from its PS is expected behavior, not an edge case.

**On tail-truncation (case 1):** The audit endpoint is governance *signaling*, not a tamper-evident complete log, and the spec doesn't claim completeness. The accountability line sits at the PS's trust decision when it grants `approved_tools` — the PS is asserting that it trusts the agent enough to act offline without per-action confirmation. An agent that silently drops audit records is outside that trust model; an agent with that threat profile shouldn't be granted `approved_tools` in the first place. A PS that needs strong audit coverage for every approved-tool action can decline to grant `approved_tools` and require per-action permission calls instead — that's an always-online governance model and it works fine for that deployment.

A sequence-counter or pre-issued nonce range would enforce completeness technically, but it would change the interaction model significantly: the PS would have to issue "work permits" before the agent acts, which undermines the offline use case that `approved_tools` enables. For PSes that want stronger guarantees, this is implementable internally without protocol changes — the PS issues nonces alongside the approved-tool grant and tracks consumption — but mandating it in the protocol would overconstrain the common case.

**On stale-mission replay (case 2):** Resource tokens have a maximum 5-minute lifetime. After the PS marks a mission revoked, it denies all new token requests referencing that mission's `s256`. A partitioned agent continues acting only until its outstanding tokens expire, at which point it must contact the PS for new ones and gets a mission-status error. The window is bounded by token lifetime — the same acknowledged tradeoff in any token-based system.

**On (b):** Sequence-counter mechanics belong at the PS implementation level, not the protocol level, for the same reason PR #10's log chaining did: the PS controls token issuance and can track what it issued without needing wire-level protocol changes. Nothing in the protocol prevents a PS from adding this.

One thing worth adding to the spec is an explicit note in the `approved_tools` section: that granting `approved_tools` is a trust decision about offline accountability, and PSes that require complete audit coverage should either not grant `approved_tools` or enforce connectivity requirements at the deployment level. That surfaces the design tradeoff without a protocol change.

If you see a gap in that reasoning — particularly around the stale-mission case or a scenario where the token-lifetime bound doesn't hold — please follow up and we can dig into it further. Otherwise I'll plan to close this in two weeks.

comments.author: ZeeshanKhanSA
comments.body:
This resolves it for me, with one residual question on case 2.

On case 1 — agreed, and I think you've put it in the right place. Completeness as a trust-model boundary at the `approved_tools` grant, rather than a wire mechanism, is the coherent call: the PS asserting offline trust and an agent that silently drops records being outside that trust model is a cleaner accountability line than a mandated counter would be. And you're right that a PS wanting guaranteed coverage has two honest options already — decline `approved_tools`, or issue-and-track nonces internally alongside the grant. That's PS-internal, same boundary as PR #10; I shouldn't have implied otherwise given I'd already called it wire-surface. The proposed `approved_tools` spec note — making the offline-accountability tradeoff explicit — is exactly the right resolution, and it's a better outcome than a protocol change.

On case 2, one thing I want to make sure I'm reading correctly. The 5-minute bound is clear for resource access — no live auth token, no resource call, and revocation denies new token requests. What I'm less sure about is a local `approved_tools` action during the partition. A pre-approved tool call — a file write, a local action, sending a message — doesn't consume a resource token or require a PS round-trip; that's the point of pre-approval. So if the mission is revoked mid-partition, what bounds the agent's continued execution of locally-authorized actions? It isn't the resource-token lifetime, since those actions don't take resource tokens — it seems to be time-to-next-PS-contact, which under partition is unbounded by design. Resource access fails safe offline; local governed action doesn't seem to have the same expiry.

If the answer is that `approved_tools` blast radius is bounded by what local tools can do — which the PS accepted when it granted them offline — then case 2 collapses into the same trust-model boundary as case 1, and I'm satisfied. I just want to confirm that's the intended reading rather than the token-lifetime bound, since they come apart exactly on the offline-local path. Either way, agreed on closing — the spec note covers the substantive gap.

comments.author: kenhuangus
comments.body:
Implementation evidence from a production-oriented AAuth implementation and conformance pass:

We found it useful to split this into two independent invariants.

1. **Permanent mission termination / stale-state detection.** We implemented a version-independent terminal tombstone written atomically with termination. Detailed mission-log ciphertext can follow a retention policy, but the minimal mission identity + terminal state is retained so an old valid mission body can never become active again after log expiry. Every create/read/mutation checks the tombstone first and returns `mission_terminated`. This closes the storage-retention form of stale-mission replay, but only at a PS that is contacted.

2. **Offline audit-tail completeness.** The tombstone does not solve the issue described here. If `approved_tools` permits work while the agent cannot reach the PS, no request-level signature archive can prove that an omitted action occurred. Our implementation therefore cannot claim complete governance evidence for offline actions.

Two small spec decisions would make this testable:

- State explicitly whether governed `approved_tools` actions MAY execute while the PS is unreachable.
- If yes, define a per-mission ordered audit commitment (monotonic sequence or PS-issued range) and the required reconciliation behavior. If no, state that governed action is online-only and failure to reach the PS blocks the action.

Suggested conformance cases:

- terminate mission, expire/delete detailed log, then replay the old mission reference => `mission_terminated`, never `not_found` or recreated;
- omit sequence N while submitting N+1 after reconnection => detectable gap;
- replay a previously accepted sequence => reject;
- reconnect after PS-side termination => agent stops before further governed action.

This supports the issue's distinction: request replay and archived signatures are necessary, but neither establishes audit-tail completeness across a partition.

issues.title: Add an explicit discriminator to pending-route agent responses (clarification response vs updated request)
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Summary

While implementing AAuth as a Rust library, an implementer noted that the two POST actions an agent can send to a pending URL in response to a clarification (clarification response and updated request) carry no explicit discriminator. They are distinguished only by which body key is present. This makes it awkward to deserialize the body into a tagged union without relying on contextual state held in the PS, or on untagged (trial) deserialization.

## Current behavior (editor's draft)

Under Clarification Chat, Agent Response to Clarification, the agent responds on the pending URL with one of:

- Cancel: `DELETE` the pending URL (disambiguated by HTTP method).
- Clarification response: `POST` a body containing `clarification_response`.
- Updated request: `POST` a body containing `resource_token` (plus optional `justification`).

The two POST variants have no tag field. A receiver determines the action only from the presence of `clarification_response` versus `resource_token`.

## Why this matters

This is not a correctness gap. The two key sets are disjoint and each variant's distinguishing key is required, so a receiver can always determine the action deterministically.

It is a deserialization ergonomics gap for statically typed implementations. Without a discriminator, the body cannot be mapped to an internally tagged enum (for example serde's `#[serde(tag = "...")]`). Implementers are pushed to untagged deserialization (variant matching by trial, weaker error messages) or manual key-presence branching.

## Proposal

Add an explicit discriminator member to the pending POST body. Reasons beyond cleanliness:

1. Symmetry with the rest of the protocol. The server-to-agent direction already tags response semantics via `requirement=` in `AAuth-Requirement`. The agent-to-server direction of the same exchange has no analogous tag.
2. The pending route is an extension point. With two POST actions and disjoint keys, untagged happens to work. A third action, or any field shared between actions, makes untagged ambiguous or order-dependent. An explicit tag keeps the route extensible.
3. Low cost now. We are pre-interop beyond the demo apps, so introducing a required discriminator is inexpensive at this stage.

Example with `action` as the discriminator (name is open, see below):

clarification response

```json
{
  "action": "clarification_response",
  "clarification_response": "I need to create a meeting invite for the participants you listed."
}
```

updated request

```json
{
  "action": "updated_request",
  "resource_token": "eyJ...",
  "justification": "I have reduced my request to read-only access."
}
```

`DELETE` remains the cancel action, so the discriminator only covers the POST body.

## Open question (field name and values)

Candidate names: `action` (parallels `requirement=` without copying it), `kind` (neutral, Rust-idiomatic), `type` (serde's default tag, but vague), `intent`. I would avoid `response_type` and `grant_type` style names, since they invite mapping AAuth back onto OAuth request grammar.

Candidate value sets:

- Long, matching the section headers and existing keys: `clarification_response` / `updated_request`.
- Short: `clarification` / `update`. Note that `clarification` as a value sits next to `requirement=clarification` on the header, so a reader has to track that one is the server's requirement and the other is the agent's response to it.

## Spec section

Clarification Chat, Agent Response to Clarification (Clarification Response, Updated Request, Cancel Request).

## Suggested labels

`spec`, `editorial`

issues.title: R3/Protocol: optional `account` parameter to bind an authorization to one of multiple accounts at a resource
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Problem

A resource that fronts multiple user accounts — e.g. an AAuth→OAuth proxy where one user has connected several Google accounts — has no way for the agent to signal *which* account an authorization applies to, and no way for the user's consent to be bound to a specific account.

The existing PS token-endpoint hints (`login_hint`, `prompt=select_account`, `domain_hint`, `tenant`) target the person's identity *at the PS*, not the selection among upstream accounts held *at the resource*. A per-call header (e.g. `Proxy-Account`) works mechanically but is unsatisfying: the consent the user approved never named the account, the auth token spans all accounts, and the audit trail can't show which account an authorization covered.

## Proposal

Add an optional `account` value that flows through the whole authorization chain:

1. **Authorization endpoint request** — new OPTIONAL parameter `account`: an identifier, chosen from the resource's account namespace (e.g. an email address for Google accounts, a portal/hub id for HubSpot), indicating which account at the resource the authorization is for. §Authorization Endpoint Request currently defines only `scope` (+ `r3_operations` in R3).

2. **R3 document** — when the request carried `account`, the resource includes a top-level `account` field and names it in `display` (e.g. "…on your Google account dick@example.com"), so the user consents to the specific account.

3. **Resource token** — new OPTIONAL claim `account`, echoing the requested account.

4. **Auth token** — the PS/AS copies `account` from the resource token into the auth token as an OPTIONAL claim. The resource enforces per-account access directly from the token — different accounts yield different auth tokens.

A PS additionally MAY use `account` at consent time to cross-check against the user's verified identifiers (e.g. "this is one of your verified emails") — a useful signal that the right person is approving.

When multiple accounts are connected and no `account` was bound, the resource can reject invocations with an error listing the connected accounts, prompting the agent to re-authorize with `account` set.

## Why not reuse `login_hint`?

`login_hint` is defined (OpenID.Core §3.1.2.1) as a hint about who to authenticate at the receiving party. Here nobody is being authenticated — the account is already connected at the resource; the parameter *selects* rather than *hints*, and it must survive into the issued tokens as a claim. Overloading `login_hint` would conflate the person logging into the PS with the account being acted on at the resource. (The resource may still internally use OAuth `login_hint` toward its upstream during a first-connect interaction flow — that's an implementation detail.)

## Proving ground

We are implementing this in the Hello AAuth proxy for Google APIs (multi Google-account support, account = email address), including the PS side. Will report back with experience; happy to PR spec text once the shape settles.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
## Implementation report-back: `account` needs a **kind** and a **label**

Promised in the "Proving ground" section. We've now implemented `account` end-to-end in the Hellō PS and the AAuth proxy, and run it past Google — QuickBooks, Threads, Slack, HubSpot. The mechanism works: the value flows request → R3 → resource token → auth token, and per-account auth tokens do give clean per-account enforcement and audit.

Two things break once the upstream is **not** email-keyed, and both trace to `account` being a bare opaque string.

### 1. The proposed PS cross-check is unsafe to implement as specified

The proposal says:

> A PS additionally MAY use `account` at consent time to cross-check against the user's verified identifiers (e.g. "this is one of your verified emails") — a useful signal that the right person is approving.

We built exactly that. It cannot be done correctly with a bare string, because the PS cannot distinguish:

1. an **email-shaped account that failed verification** — a real signal worth showing, from
2. an **opaque provider id that was never an email** — unknowable, and the common case

Our check could only ever match subjects of kind `email`, so everything in case 2 fell into the negative branch. Connecting a QuickBooks sandbox company rendered:

> on the account **9341457618438679**
> ⚠️ Note: This is not one of your verified email addresses.

…on every consent, for every id-keyed resource. A non-blocking warning that fires constantly for legitimate reasons is worse than no warning — it trains people to ignore the one case where it means something.

**We have removed the negative rendering** (kept the positive "one of your verified emails" chip, which has no false-positive mode). Tracked as hellocoop/Wallet#4106.

Suggest the spec say plainly that the cross-check is only defined when the account is an email — which requires the PS to be able to *tell*, hence:

### 2. Consent cards can't render an opaque id usefully

`9341457618438679` is a QuickBooks realmId. The user has no idea whether that is their sandbox company or someone else's. Same for a Slack `T…` team id or a Threads app-scoped id. The card names the account, per the proposal's intent — but names it in a way the person cannot recognise, which undercuts the point of binding consent to a specific account.

The proxy *has* human labels ("Sandbox Company US 0a7d", "@dickhardt on Threads"); there's simply nowhere on the wire to put them.

### Proposed shape

Make `account` structured (keeping the bare string as the shorthand for `kind: "email"`, or as a deprecated form):

```json
"account": {
  "id":    "9341457618438679",
  "kind":  "id",
  "label": "Sandbox Company US 0a7d"
}
```

- **`id`** — the wire identifier; what the resource enforces on, unchanged from today.
- **`kind`** — `email` | `id`, extensible. Lets a PS run the verified-identifier cross-check *only* when it is meaningful, and stay silent otherwise.
- **`label`** — OPTIONAL human-readable string for display. Consent cards should render label-first and never show a bare opaque id.

For `kind: "email"` the label is typically the address itself, so Google-style upstreams are unchanged in appearance.

### Also affects the account-selection error

The proposal's "reject invocations listing the connected accounts" has the same problem. Ours is currently:

```ts
{ kind: 'account_required'; accounts: string[] }   // proxies/core/token-provider.ts
```

An agent surfacing that list to a user shows a column of opaque ids. Whatever shape `account` settles on should be reused here, so selection and consent are both label-first with ids on the wire.

### Summary

The account extension is right; it's just under-specified for non-email namespaces. `kind` is the load-bearing addition — without it, a PS cannot safely implement the cross-check the proposal already invites. `label` is what makes the consent legible.

Happy to PR spec text for the structured form plus the `account_required` listing.

issues.title: sign .well-known document fetches
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body: would allow a server to provide different metadata for different requesters to allow configuration that is requester specific

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
Writing this up as a design discussion rather than spec text — **not targeted at the next version.** Pros and cons below; the open questions at the bottom are the ones that decide it.

## The use case

The motivating case is R3. `r3_vocabularies` maps vocabulary URIs to *discovery endpoints*:

```json
"r3_vocabularies": {
  "urn:aauth:vocabulary:mcp": "https://calendar.example.com/mcp",
  "urn:aauth:vocabulary:openapi": "https://calendar.example.com/openapi.json"
}
```

For a gateway or a resource with a tiered API surface, the answer to "which vocabularies, and which MCP endpoint" is legitimately requester-specific — different agents see a different tool surface. That is not a configuration nicety; it is the resource's authorization surface, and today there is no way to express it.

The same shape applies to `scope_descriptions` and plausibly to future capability members.

## Two mechanisms

**Query parameter.** The approach taken in some recent OAuth work — append a parameter to the `.well-known` URL and let the server vary the response.

**HTTP Message Signature on the fetch.** The agent signs the `GET` per the AAuth profile, presenting its agent token via `Signature-Key`. The resource verifies and tailors.

The signed request is strictly stronger for AAuth's purposes:

- A query parameter is an **unauthenticated claim**. Anyone can assert any value, so a resource can only ever treat it as a hint — never as the basis for disclosing a narrower or broader surface.
- A signed request carries a **verified** agent identity, so the resource can genuinely gate what it discloses.
- AAuth agents already sign every request. There is no new client machinery — this is the one protocol where the client always holds a key.
- It stays inside AAuth's existing verification path; no new parameter to register, no cache-key semantics to define in the URL.

## Pros

- Solves the R3 vocabulary case properly, with authentication rather than an unauthenticated hint.
- Zero new machinery on the agent side.
- Composes with the existing `AAuth-Capabilities` request header — a resource could tailor on declared capabilities *and* verified identity in the same request.
- Keeps one URL. No second endpoint to advertise, discover, and version.

## Cons

**1. Bootstrap circularity — the one that constrains the design.**

The `.well-known` document is what a verifier fetches *in order to discover keys*. Agent signs its metadata fetch → resource verifies → resource fetches the AP's `aauth-agent.json` to get the AP's JWKS. If metadata fetches could themselves *require* signatures, this recurses.

It terminates only if signing a metadata fetch is **always OPTIONAL** and the unsigned response is **always valid and complete**. That has to be an explicit invariant, not an implication.

**2. Caching.**

§JWKS Discovery and Caching mandates caching with a once-per-minute fetch floor and a 24h ceiling. Those rules assume one document per issuer. A resource's metadata is also fetched by parties that are **not** the agent — PSes and ASes verifying resource tokens — who have no agent identity to present and need the stable public view.

**3. Tracking.**

HTTP Signature Keys §Key Discovery Tracking already flags metadata fetches as a side channel. Signing upgrades "someone is about to call you" to "agent X, acting for person Y, is about to call you" — disclosed *before* the agent has committed to making a request. That is a real regression in a protocol that otherwise works hard at directed identifiers, and it is not obviously worth it for a vocabulary list.

**4. Interaction with the `issuer` check.**

draft-hardt-httpbis-signature-key-08 requires the metadata document to carry `issuer` and requires verifiers to compare it byte-for-byte against the identity the document was fetched under. A varying document does not break this *provided* `issuer` itself never varies — but it makes the invariant load-bearing in a way it is not today.

## Proposed shape, if we do it — split by stability, not by endpoint

- **Stable core — MUST be byte-identical in the signed and unsigned views:** `issuer`, `jwks_uri`, `token_endpoint` / `authorization_endpoint`, `access_mode`. This keeps the `issuer` byte-equality check and all key caching valid regardless of who asks.
- **MAY vary by verified requester when the request is signed:** `r3_vocabularies`, `scope_descriptions`, future capability members.
- **An unsigned fetch MUST return a complete, usable document** — the resource's public default view. This is what closes the bootstrap circularity.
- **Signed responses MUST carry `Cache-Control: private`** and MUST NOT be entered into the shared JWKS/metadata cache. The stable core may still be cached from the unsigned view.

## The alternative worth weighing against it

A separate capabilities endpoint, advertised **in** the stable metadata, that is signed and never cached. Costs one extra round trip and one metadata member; needs no special rules at all — no split-document invariant, no cache-mode distinction, no bootstrap caveat. The complexity budget is meaningfully lower.

The case for the single-URL version is that the extra hop is paid by every agent on every resource, forever, to avoid rules that are written once.

## Open questions

1. Is the tracking cost acceptable? A signed metadata fetch discloses intent-to-call before the call. Is that materially different from the call itself, given the agent was going to make it anyway — or does it matter that an agent may fetch metadata for resources it then decides not to use?
2. Does the stable-core invariant hold up under review, or are there members not on the list that a verifier other than the agent depends on?
3. Is the single-URL saving worth the split-document rules, versus a separate signed capabilities endpoint?
4. Does this belong in the AAuth protocol draft at all, or in R3 — since the motivating member (`r3_vocabularies`) is R3's?

Related: the OAuth WG has recent work proposing a query parameter on `.well-known` for request-specific responses; worth reading their rationale alongside this, and worth raising the signed-fetch alternative there, since it is strictly stronger for any client that holds a key.

comments.body:
## The OAuth WG precedent: draft-watson-oauth-as-metadata-client-id

Link: https://njwatson32.github.io/as-metadata-client-id/draft-watson-oauth-as-metadata-client-id.html

Having read it, it both **supports** the general shape and **sharpens why AAuth should take the signed variant rather than the query-parameter one.**

### What it defines

An OPTIONAL `client_id` query parameter on the authorization server metadata endpoint (`/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`). The AS MAY customize the metadata response — including response headers such as `Cache-Control` — based on the identified client.

Two graceful-degradation rules do most of the work:

- An AS that does not recognize the client, or declines to customize, **MUST ignore the parameter and return the standard global metadata**.
- A client **should gracefully handle a 400 and retry without the parameter**, since a non-adopting server may reject an unknown query parameter.

### Its rationale is operational, not authorization-shaped

The motivation is deployment risk: "authorization servers frequently undergo configuration updates or feature additions where a global rollout carries significant risk." The named use cases are **phased rollouts, canary testing, and per-client deprecations** — serving beta features selectively, keeping legacy methods alive for incompatible clients, migrating endpoints gradually.

That is a real need and AAuth has it too. But it is a *different* need from ours. AAuth's motivating case is `r3_vocabularies` — which tool surface a given agent is even allowed to see. Watson's variation is about *rollout timing* for a document that is otherwise the same for everyone; ours is about *content that legitimately differs per requester and is security-relevant*.

That distinction matters for the next point.

### Its own security consideration is the argument for signing

The draft names the weakness directly: because the request is unauthenticated, an attacker can "query the metadata endpoint with arbitrary client identifiers" and "learn specific client configurations." It accepts this, reasoning that AS metadata is typically public anyway and warning only that sensitive business logic could leak through client-specific variation.

**That reasoning holds for their use case and does not hold for ours.** If a resource varies `r3_vocabularies` per agent, the variation *is* the sensitive part — enumerating agent identifiers would enumerate the tool surfaces the resource exposes to each of them. An unauthenticated parameter cannot carry that; a signed request can.

So the precedent reads as: the OAuth WG has confirmed the need, chosen the unauthenticated mechanism because OAuth clients do not universally hold keys at metadata-fetch time, and explicitly booked the resulting disclosure as an accepted cost. AAuth is not in that position — its agents always hold a key and already sign every request — so it can have the same capability without the cost.

### What we should borrow regardless of mechanism

Two patterns from the draft are better than what I proposed above, and apply to the signed variant unchanged:

1. **Ignore-and-fall-back, rather than error.** A server that does not recognize the requester, or declines to vary, MUST return the standard document. This is a stronger form of the "unsigned fetch MUST return a complete, usable document" invariant — it means the *signed* path also degrades to the public view rather than failing, so an agent never has to reason about whether tailoring happened.
2. **Per-response cache control is explicitly in scope.** The draft contemplates the server varying `Cache-Control` alongside the body, which is precedent for the `Cache-Control: private` requirement on tailored responses.

The client-side "retry without the parameter on 400" rule has no analogue we need: an unsigned AAuth metadata fetch is the default, so the fallback is simply not signing.

### Updated open question

The earlier open question 3 — single URL versus a separate signed capabilities endpoint — is now better framed as:

> Does AAuth want the *operational* variation Watson is solving for (rollout, canary, deprecation), the *authorization-surface* variation R3 needs, or both? The first is well served by an unauthenticated hint and could adopt Watson's parameter directly if it advances. The second needs authentication and is the only one that forces the split-document rules.

If the answer is "both," they may be two mechanisms rather than one, and conflating them is how the split-document invariant gets harder than it needs to be.

issues.title: Use Ed25519 rather than the deprecated polymorphic EdDSA alg identifier
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
AAuth uses the polymorphic JOSE identifier `EdDSA` as the `alg` value throughout. RFC 9864 (Jones and Steele, Standards Track, October 2025) deprecates that identifier in the JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms registry and registers fully-specified replacements: `Ed25519` and `Ed448`.

AAuth should move to `Ed25519`.

## Why this matters for AAuth specifically

AAuth depends normatively on HTTP Signature Keys (`[@!I-D.hardt-httpbis-signature-key]`, 24 citations in the protocol draft alone). That draft is adding an Algorithm Determination rule requiring every conveyed or referenced JWK to carry a present, fully-specified `alg`, and forbidding the polymorphic `EdDSA` identifier outright (dickhardt/signature-key#19).

Once that lands, AAuth's current text is non-conformant with its own normative dependency.

## The load-bearing one

`draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol.md:2333`:

> Agents and resources MUST support EdDSA using Ed25519 ([@!RFC8032]).

This is exactly the pattern RFC 9864 deprecates: a polymorphic algorithm name with the curve pinned separately in prose. A verifier reading only the `alg` value cannot tell Ed25519 from Ed448. Under the fully-specified rule this becomes:

> Agents and resources MUST support Ed25519 ([@!RFC8032]).

and the curve no longer needs a separate prose sentence, because the identifier carries it.

## All sites

**`draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol.md`** (5)
- L538 — "The agent generates a signing key pair (EdDSA is RECOMMENDED)."
- L549 — "`alg`: Signing algorithm. EdDSA is RECOMMENDED."
- L790 — same, resource tokens
- L1661 — same, auth tokens
- L2333 — the MUST-support statement above

**`draft-hardt-aauth-events.md`** (2)
- L218, L354 — "`alg`: Signing algorithm. EdDSA is RECOMMENDED."

**`draft-hardt-aauth-r3.md`** (3)
- L417, L489 — `"alg": "EdDSA"` in JWT header examples
- L668 — changelog entry, historical record, leave as-is

**`draft-hardt-aauth-bootstrap.md`** (1)
- L255 — `{ "alg": "EdDSA", "typ": "aa-agent+jwt", "kid": "..." }`

Ten sites to change; the L668 changelog line is a historical record and should stay.

## Related

#58 proposes a metadata field declaring which algorithms a server **accepts** from clients, which is a separate direction from what it signs with. The two interact: values in that field should be fully-specified identifiers, which is what this issue is about.

issues.title: Metadata should declare which signing algorithms a server accepts, not just what it signs with
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
AAuth has no metadata field declaring which signing algorithms a server will **accept** from clients. This is a different question from what it signs with, and only the latter is currently answerable.

- **What a server signs with** is declared by `jwks_uri`. Each JWK carries `kty`/`crv`/`alg`, so fetching the JWKS answers it. AAuth correctly has no separate list for this; it would be redundant.
- **What a server accepts** on incoming agent-signed requests and tokens is declared nowhere.

The only `*_supported` fields in AAuth today are `scopes_supported` and `claims_supported`, both PS-only, and neither is about algorithms.

## Why this matters for AAuth specifically

Today an agent learns a server's accepted algorithms only reactively: sign, get rejected, read the list, retry. HTTP Signature Keys defines that path and requires the feedback member, so it does work:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Signature-Error: error=unsupported_algorithm,
    supported_algorithms=("Ed25519" "ES256")
```

But it costs a round trip and a failure on first contact, which cuts against AAuth's premise that an agent can act with no pre-registration. An agent that holds several keys, or that can generate one on demand, has no way to pick a conformant one before its first request. It has to guess, fail, and retry.

The reactive path should stay regardless. This is about letting an agent skip the failure when the server has bothered to say.

## Precedent: RFC 9728 already makes this exact distinction

AAuth's metadata section already discusses RFC 9728 and notes where it deliberately diverges. RFC 9728 defines both directions as separate parameters:

| Parameter | Direction |
|---|---|
| `resource_signing_alg_values_supported` | algorithms the resource uses **signing its own responses** |
| `dpop_signing_alg_values_supported` | algorithms the resource **accepts when validating** client-signed DPoP proof JWTs |

The second is the close analog. A DPoP proof is a client-signed proof-of-possession JWT the server validates — structurally the same situation as an agent-signed HTTP Message Signature or agent token in AAuth. RFC 9728 treats "what I accept from you" as worth its own parameter, distinct from "what I sign with."

## Proposal

Add an OPTIONAL field to the shared metadata table, so all four documents (`aauth-agent.json`, `aauth-resource.json`, `aauth-person.json`, `aauth-access.json`) get it. Every role verifies inbound signatures, so every role has an answer.

Naming, following the `*_alg_values_supported` convention but in AAuth's unprefixed style:

- `request_signing_alg_values_supported` — names the direction explicitly. Preferred.
- `signature_alg_values_supported` — shorter, but does not say which direction.
- `accepted_signing_alg_values` — unambiguous, but breaks the convention.

Semantics roughly: a JSON array of JWS `alg` values the server accepts when verifying signatures on inbound requests and tokens. OPTIONAL; when absent, a client discovers the set reactively via `unsupported_algorithm`. When present it is advisory, not a contract, and a server still returns `unsupported_algorithm` for anything it declines.

## Interaction with fully-specified algorithms

Values here should be fully-specified identifiers (`Ed25519`, not `EdDSA`) per #57 and the Algorithm Determination rule in HTTP Signature Keys (dickhardt/signature-key#19).

That rule makes this field more useful than it would otherwise be: since a fully-specified `alg` determines the key type and curve, a list like `("Ed25519" "ES256")` tells the agent not just which algorithms are acceptable but which **keys** to generate. `EdDSA` would not, since it leaves Ed25519 and Ed448 ambiguous.

issues.title: Revocation endpoint must identify tokens by issuer + jti, not jti alone
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
A \`jti\` is only unique within a single issuer. A revocation endpoint that accepts just a \`jti\` cannot unambiguously identify which token is being revoked when the revoking party holds tokens from multiple issuers (multiple PSes, multiple resources), and it opens the door to cross-issuer collisions — revoking (or failing to revoke) the wrong token.

The revocation request must carry the **token issuer as well as the jti** so the pair \`(iss, jti)\` uniquely identifies the token being revoked. Recipients maintaining revocation state should key it by that pair.

issues.title: PS should expose an agent token revocation endpoint
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
The PS issues tokens to agents (auth tokens bound to the agent's key), but there is currently no defined way for those tokens to be revoked before they expire.

The PS should expose an **agent token revocation endpoint** so that issued agent tokens can be invalidated — e.g. when a user withdraws a grant, an agent key is compromised, or an agent is decommissioned. Tokens should be identified by \`(iss, jti)\` per #59.

Considerations:
- Who may call it: the agent itself (self-revocation), the user via the PS UI, and potentially the resource.
- How resources learn of revocation: since auth tokens are verified by signature without a PS round trip, revocation implies either short token lifetimes, a status/introspection mechanism, or resource-side revocation lists.

issues.title: Companion draft: sharing activity and compromise signals between AAuth parties
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Spun out of the `-10` revocation work. An OPTIONAL `revocation_endpoint` was briefly added to agent provider metadata; it has been removed again, because revocation is the wrong shape for what it was reaching for.

## What revocation does and does not cover

Revocation is now well defined for the tokens a party issues: the PS or AS calls the resource's `revocation_endpoint`, and the AP calls the **PS's** `revocation_endpoint` for an agent token, finding the PS from the `ps` claim it placed in that token. In each case the caller is the issuer, acting on its own decision.

What it does not cover is a party telling another party something it should act on:

- A PS observes an agent behaving anomalously and wants to tell the AP. The PS cannot revoke an agent token — it is not the issuer — and forcing the AP's hand would invert the AP's role as the policy enforcement point for its own fleet.
- A resource sees abuse from an agent and has no channel to the PS or the AP beyond refusing the request.
- An AP learns a fleet-wide key or supply-chain compromise and wants to warn the PSes its agents use, ahead of, or instead of, revoking token by token.

These are reports, not commands. The recipient decides what to do.

## Why an endpoint on the AP was the wrong answer

Revoking a token buys at most the remaining agent token lifetime — 24 hours at most, per the agent token `exp` guidance. The agent then re-proves its identity to the AP by the platform-specific mechanism and renews. The durable action is the AP declining to issue again, which is a policy decision at the AP and needs no endpoint of its own. And because an auth token's `exp` cannot exceed the agent token's, and a resource must reject an auth token whose agent token has expired, declining renewal already propagates to every resource within that window without any revocation call.

So the missing piece is not another revocation endpoint. It is a signal channel.

## Scope for a companion draft

- Signal types: suspected compromise, anomalous behaviour, decommissioning, key compromise, fleet-wide advisories.
- Direction: PS to AP, resource to PS, resource to AP, AP to PS. Each party reports what it observes to a party that can act.
- Semantics: a signal is evidence, never an instruction. The recipient evaluates it under its own policy.
- Relationship to [AAuth Events](https://github.com/dickhardt/AAuth/blob/main/draft-hardt-aauth-events.md), which already carries event tokens to an AP's `event_endpoint` — this may belong there rather than in a new document.
- Relationship to CAEP / SSF, which solve a close-enough problem that reuse should be considered before inventing anything.
- Privacy: a signal identifies an agent, and often a person by implication. What may be disclosed to whom, and what the recipient may retain.

## Not blocking

Nothing here is needed for the current version. Filed so the design question is not lost.

issues.title: OpenAPI Gateway vocabulary for resources fronting multiple services
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Removed from R3 before publication, to be settled before it goes back in. The operation identifier scope rules it accompanied are unaffected and remain in the draft.

## The problem it addressed

A resource that fronts several OpenAPI-described backend services behind one resource identifier — an API gateway — cannot use the plain `urn:aauth:vocabulary:openapi` vocabulary cleanly. That vocabulary assumes one OpenAPI document per resource, and `operationId` is unique only within a document, so two services can each define `createEvent` and a bare identifier no longer resolves.

R3 currently requires such a resource to do one of two things (#operation-identifier-scope):

- present the services as one valid definition at the discovery endpoint, renaming colliding identifiers, or
- expose them under separate resource identifiers, letting the auth token's `aud` distinguish them.

Both are workable. Neither is free: the first pushes a rename burden onto the gateway and breaks identifier parity with the upstream services, the second multiplies resource identifiers for what an operator thinks of as one resource.

## What was removed

A third vocabulary, `urn:aauth:vocabulary:openapi-gateway`, where:

- the `r3_vocabularies` discovery value is a JSON object mapping service labels to OpenAPI spec URLs rather than a single URL;
- each operation entry is a (`service`, `operationId`) pair;
- `operationId` need only be unique within one service's specification.

## Why it was pulled

- **It is the only vocabulary whose discovery value is not a URL.** That special case leaked into the general `r3_vocabularies` description, which had to say a vocabulary MAY define a structured discovery value. One vocabulary should not reshape the metadata contract for all of them.
- **Service labels become grant-bearing identifiers.** They are resource-chosen, appear in R3 documents and auth token claims, and relabeling silently invalidates existing grants even when the underlying specification has not changed. The draft said labels SHOULD be stable, which states the hazard without resolving it.
- **The pattern is not OpenAPI-specific.** A gateway fronting several MCP servers or several gRPC services has the same collision. Solving it once per vocabulary does not scale; if qualification is the answer it likely belongs in the operation entry structure generally, or in the discovery layer, rather than as a parallel vocabulary per format.

## To decide

1. Is multi-service aggregation behind one resource identifier a case R3 should support directly, or is "use separate resource identifiers" the right answer and the gateway case simply out of scope?
2. If supported, is qualification per-vocabulary (a `-gateway` variant for each format) or general (an optional qualifier in operation entries across all vocabularies)?
3. Whatever carries the qualifier, what makes grants survive relabeling — or is label stability simply a deployment requirement stated normatively?

Implementer input from anyone running a gateway in front of AAuth resources would be especially useful here.

issues.title: Add a person token: identify the person to a resource before authorization
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
An agent token identifies the agent, not the person it acts for. Until the PS issues an auth token, a resource has no way to learn who the person is, so anything it records is keyed on an agent identifier that a change of agent provider replaces.

**Proposal.** A PS-issued JWT, `typ: aa-person+jwt`, audience-restricted to one resource, carrying a directed `sub`. Presented via `Signature-Key` in place of the agent token. Obtained from a new `person_token_endpoint`, REQUIRED in PS metadata. Lifetime capped at 1 hour, matching auth tokens.

**It carries no authorization from the PS, but that does not mean it grants nothing.** A resource may serve requests on identity alone, and where it does, holding a person token is effectively access — the same position an ID token puts you in after a login. The consent question at first issuance is therefore whether this agent may *act at* the resource as the person, not whether it may name them.

**Why an agent identifier was the wrong thing to be sending.** Each agent belongs to exactly one person and presents the same agent token everywhere, so `aauth:local@domain` is a globally correlatable pseudonym for the person, handed to every resource on first contact along with the agent provider's domain. A directed `sub` scoped to one resource discloses strictly less.

Implemented in #73.

issues.title: Require a person token to obtain a resource token
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Only a person server can act on a resource token — it is the audience in three-party, and in four-party it is the only party permitted to call the AS token endpoint. A resource token issued to an agent that cannot name a person is one nobody can redeem.

**Proposal.** A resource MUST have verified a person token before issuing a resource token, and challenges with `requirement=person-token` when it has not.

**What it costs.** The proactive authorization endpoint becomes unavailable to agents with no person server, and the `401` path gains one round trip on first contact for agents that do not read `access_mode`. Agent identity access and resource-managed access remain open to PS-less agents, so nothing is closed off to them that they could have used — an agent with no PS could never have redeemed a resource token.

**What it buys.** Every resource token now carries the person the resource actually verified, which is what lets the agent identifier come out of the resource-facing tokens entirely, and what makes the mission PS-asserted rather than agent-asserted.

Implemented in #73.

issues.title: Five resource access modes instead of four
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
The access modes were presented as a ladder of protocol adoption. With the person token there is a fifth rung, and a better organising question: what does the resource need to know before it serves a request, and which party established it?

| Mode | Resource knows | Established by |
|---|---|---|
| Agent identity | which agent | the agent provider |
| Resource-managed | which person | the resource own flow |
| Person identity | which person | the person server |
| PS authorization | person and consented scope | the person server |
| Federated authorization | person and policy verdict | the access server |

Resource-managed and person-identity reach the same destination by different routes — local login versus federated login — which is why they stay distinct.

A resource applies different modes to different endpoints, and that is the expected shape rather than an edge case: most calls need only identity, a few sensitive operations warrant an authorization decision.

Touches the abstract, the protocol overview, the adoption matrix, and incremental adoption. Implemented in #73.

issues.title: Remove agent identity from every token a resource reads
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
A resource that pins state or policy to an agent identifier loses that state when the person changes agent provider, and can condition access on which agent product is calling — which makes agent providers gatekeepers.

**Proposal.** No agent identifier in the person token, the resource token, or the auth token. `agent_jkt` and `cnf` remain the binding to one key.

**The exception, stated deliberately.** The agent token still reaches the AS as a REQUIRED parameter, because a resource deploys an AS to have policy evaluated and an agent token may carry claims bearing on that — attestation, platform integrity, workload identity. The resource enforces; the AS evaluates; posture goes to the evaluator.

The consequence is that agent-provider independence is complete in three-party and partial in four-party, where the resource has explicitly delegated policy to an access server. The specification should claim the property accurately rather than universally.

Implemented in #73.

issues.title: Remove the act claim and the delegation chain
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
The `act` claim recorded the chain of agents upstream of the presenter. It served no reader.

In call chaining the immediate caller signs the request with its own key and presents its own credentials, so a downstream resource already knows who is calling. `act` named the parties one and two hops further up — parties the downstream has no relationship with and cannot evaluate. Those parties are also the person tooling, disclosed to a resource that did not need them.

The chain is held by the person server, which authorizes every hop and holds the mission log. The same reasoning that stopped resources attributing missions applies: the resource enforces, the person server attributes.

**No interop cost.** RFC 8693 `act` names the *current* actor — the party authorized to act on the subject behalf. AAuth put the *upstream* party there and swapped `sub` for `agent`, so it was already a different claim wearing the same name.

**What goes with it.** The Delegation Chain section and its examples, the `act` steps in auth token verification and delivery, and the `act` construction in upstream token verification. Sub-agent structure stops being visible downstream and is held by the person server, which issued both tokens.

Implemented in #73.

issues.title: Remove the AAuth-Mission header; missions travel only in PS-issued tokens
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Any agent could put any value in `AAuth-Mission` and no resource could check it. A resource that records the mission for forensics was recording an agent assertion.

**Proposal.** The mission reaches a resource only inside a person token, which the person server issued after validating that the mission exists, is active, and belongs to that agent. The resource copies it into the resource token, and it flows into the auth token. `mission_s256` replaces the `{approver, s256}` object; `approver` is dropped everywhere but the mission blob, since the person server is identified by `ps`.

**A mission cannot exist without a person**, so any agent operating under one has a person server and can obtain a person token. There is no request that needs to carry a mission but cannot carry the person — which is what made the header removable rather than merely undesirable.

**Mission stripping.** A resource could still omit `mission_s256`. The resource token names the person token by `jti`, so the person server resolves what it actually issued and compares. Comparing claims alone would not work: concurrent missions mean several person tokens per agent and resource, so "the person token for this pair" does not identify one.

Implemented in #73.

issues.title: Rename token_endpoint to auth_token_endpoint
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
With `person_token_endpoint` alongside it, a bare `token_endpoint` no longer says which token it issues. The pair `auth_token_endpoint` / `person_token_endpoint` names itself.

**This diverges from OAuth and OpenID Connect vocabulary, against the document own rationale for reusing it.** Raising it separately because it is the one change in #73 that contradicts a stated design principle, and it should be decided on its own rather than carried in on the back of the person token.

The argument for doing it anyway: AAuth token endpoint does not behave like OAuth — no grant types, no client authentication, signed POST, deferred responses — so the shared name was asserting a similarity that is not there. And there are no known implementations, so this is the last free moment.

Applies to both PS and AS metadata. The AS has only one token endpoint and no ambiguity to resolve; it renames for symmetry, which is the weaker half of the case.

Implemented in #73.

issues.title: Mission sub-resource has no error model, and would leak mission existence
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Protocol -11 added `POST {mission_endpoint}/{mission_s256}` for `action: update` and `action: completion`. It specifies `400` for a missing or unrecognized `action` and nothing else.

Unspecified: what a PS returns when the mission does not exist, when it exists but belongs to a different agent, and when the path segment is malformed.

**Why the first two must be indistinguishable.** `mission_s256` travels in auth tokens to resources. A resource operator running an agent could POST to the PS with a mission reference it observed and learn from the response whether that mission is still live — reading mission status through a side channel rather than through the control plane, where the read would be authorized. Distinguishing "no such mission" from "not yours" turns the agent surface into an existence oracle.

**Proposed:**

| Case | Response |
|---|---|
| Mission does not exist | `404` `mission_not_found` |
| Exists, not this agent's | `404` `mission_not_found` — identical body, headers, and timing |
| This agent's, terminated | `403` `mission_terminated` with `termination_reason` (already specified) |
| Malformed `{mission_s256}` | `400` `invalid_request`, rejected before lookup |

Plus: rate-limit and security-log repeated failures without retaining raw references longer than needed, and state that the authorization check must not short-circuit before the lookup for one case and after it for the other — the natural implementation leaks the timing.

Terminated stays deliberately distinguishable: the agent owns that mission, already knew it existed, and needs the reason to decide whether to propose a new one.

The anti-oracle rule is Karl McGuinness's, specified for the mission control plane in `draft-mcguinness-mission-aauth-management`. It applies unchanged to the agent surface.

issues.title: Person token: the PS's retention obligation is implied but never stated
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Resource Token Verification step 6 says:

> A PS MUST look up the person token identified by `person_token_jti` among those it issued, and MUST verify that `ps`, `sub`, `mission_s256`, and `tenant` match that token exactly, rejecting the resource token on any mismatch or omission.

"look up ... among those it issued" makes every PS stateful about the person tokens it has issued. That is new storage on the hot path of every token request, and the document never says so.

Three things are missing:

1. **The retention requirement is never stated.** Person Token Endpoint and Person Token Structure describe issuance as if the token were self-contained. An implementer reading those sections would not know they had been handed a storage requirement; they discover it only in a verification step in a different section, phrased as an aside.

2. **There is no retention floor.** Must the record outlive the resource token's 5 minutes, or the person token's 1 hour? Neither bound is stated. A PS that discards the record at, say, 10 minutes would fail resource tokens presented late within the person token's validity, and nothing in the document tells it that is wrong. The interaction with deferred flows makes this worse: a resource token can expire while user interaction is pending, the agent re-fetches, and the same person token is referenced much later.

3. **The absent-record case has no distinct error.** Step 6 says "rejecting the resource token on any mismatch or omission", which conflates two different conditions: the PS has the record and the claims disagree (evidence of tampering, e.g. mission stripping), versus the PS has no record at all (could be tampering, could be the PS's own retention window expiring, could be a `jti` from another PS). These deserve different error codes and probably different operator alerting.

Suggested fix: state the obligation in Person Token Endpoint or Person Token Structure — a PS MUST retain enough of each issued person token (`jti`, `ps`, `sub`, `mission_s256`, `tenant`, `exp`) to answer step 6, for at least the token's lifetime — and split the step 6 error into "unknown person token" and "person token claim mismatch".

issues.title: Nothing selects the tenant for a person token
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
The `tenant` claim has a complete lifecycle everywhere except at the point where its value is chosen.

- Person Token Structure: `tenant` is an OPTIONAL claim, "declaring the organization the person belongs to".
- Resource Token Structure: `tenant` is "Copied from the person token when it carried one."
- Resource Token Verification step 6: the PS "MUST verify that `ps`, `sub`, `mission_s256`, and `tenant` match that token exactly, rejecting the resource token on any mismatch or omission."

So the value is fixed at person-token issuance and enforced by exact match thereafter. But Person Token Endpoint defines only `resource`, `mission_s256`, `subagent_token`, and `upstream_token`. There is no `tenant` parameter, no `domain_hint`, and no default rule.

A person commonly holds more than one context — a personal one plus one or more managed organizations. The PS must pick one at issuance time, before the resource has said anything about which it wants, with no input from the agent and no stated default. Whatever it picks is then locked in by step 6's exact match: the resource cannot correct it, and the agent cannot request a different one without some way to ask.

Note the asymmetry: the PS token endpoint *does* accept `tenant` and `domain_hint`. But by the time the agent reaches the PS token endpoint it is carrying a resource token whose `tenant` was already copied from the person token, and step 6 will reject any resource token whose `tenant` does not match. The parameters that exist are on the endpoint where the decision has already been made.

Either the person token endpoint needs a `tenant` request parameter (and probably `domain_hint` alongside it, for symmetry with the PS token endpoint), or the document needs to state a default — e.g. the person's personal context unless the mission or an `upstream_token` establishes otherwise — and say how an agent obtains a person token for a different one.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
## Proposed resolution (from the document author)

**The person token endpoint accepts the same request parameters as the auth token endpoint.**

One edit closes this issue and #89 together. Both are the same defect seen from different sides: the person token endpoint was given a four-parameter list when it needed the auth token endpoint's list.

### The two endpoints have the same shape

This is the substance of the argument, not a convenience case for reuse. §Person Token Endpoint and §Agent Token Request describe endpoints that do the same kinds of thing:

- Either can return `202` with `requirement=interaction`.
- Either may need to establish which person the agent acts for.
- Either renders a consent screen to that person.
- Either creates or updates an entry in the PS's connected-agents dashboard.

Every parameter that exists to serve that flow at the auth token endpoint serves the same flow at the person token endpoint. §Agent Token Request defines:

> `resource_token`, `upstream_token`, `subagent_token`, `justification`, `login_hint`, `tenant`, `domain_hint`, `prompt`, `platform`, `device`, `capabilities`
