issues.title: No way to convey capabilities to the person token endpoint
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
A PS that wants to interact with the person before issuing its first person token has no conformant way to learn whether the agent can drive an interaction.

Three statements in the document combine to close every path:

1. **The header is ruled out.** §AAuth-Capabilities Request Header: "Agents SHOULD include the `AAuth-Capabilities` header on signed requests to resources. The header is not used on requests to PS endpoints: on the PS token endpoint the agent conveys capabilities via the `capabilities` request parameter, and within a mission the PS also has the capabilities captured at mission approval."

2. **The parameter does not exist.** §Person Token Endpoint defines exactly four request parameters: `resource` (REQUIRED), `mission_s256` (OPTIONAL), `subagent_token` (OPTIONAL), `upstream_token` (OPTIONAL). There is no `capabilities`. The PS token endpoint has one; the person token endpoint does not.

3. **The PS is nonetheless expected to interact here.** §Person Token Endpoint: "The PS MAY require user interaction before issuing and return a `202 Accepted` deferred response with `requirement=interaction`."

The mission fallback named in (1) does not close the gap. `mission_s256` is OPTIONAL on this endpoint, and first contact with a resource commonly has no mission at all — an agent working outside a mission, or one that has not yet proposed a mission, reaches the person token endpoint with nothing that carries capabilities.

## Why this is the common path, not an edge case

The same section frames interaction at first issuance as the expected behaviour:

> Because a resource MAY serve requests on identity alone, the question put to the person is whether this agent may act at the resource as them, not merely whether it may name them. A PS SHOULD fetch the resource's metadata before issuing for a resource the person has not used, and present its `name`, `description`, and `access_mode` so that the person is answering the question the resource will actually apply.

So the design intends a PS to put a question to the person the first time an agent asks for a person token for a new resource. That is precisely the request on which the PS cannot tell whether a `202` with `requirement=interaction` is actionable or a dead end. A PS that guesses wrong either blocks an agent that could have driven the interaction, or returns a `202` to an agent that will never complete it.

## Likely direction, not a resolution

The obvious fix is a `capabilities` request parameter on the person token endpoint, defined exactly parallel to the one on the PS token endpoint — OPTIONAL, an array of values from the AAuth Capability Value Registry, with the same mission fallback when `mission_s256` is present.

The other option is to relax the header rule for this endpoint and let `AAuth-Capabilities` travel on person token endpoint requests.

Which is right depends on a question the document does not currently answer: is `AAuth-Capabilities` resource-only **by principle** — because a PS request is a body-carrying POST and capabilities belong with the other request parameters — or resource-only **by circumstance**, because the two PS endpoints that existed when the rule was written both happened to have a parameter? If the former, add the parameter. If the latter, the header rule is the thing that is wrong and should be narrowed rather than worked around.

## Known implementation divergence

The reference implementation currently sends the `AAuth-Capabilities` header on person token endpoint requests. This contradicts statement (1) above. It was done deliberately: the alternative is a PS that cannot tell whether a `202` it returns is actionable. Flagging it here as a known divergence pending this decision, so it is not mistaken for an oversight.

## Related

Two other gaps at the same endpoint: #87 (the PS's person-token retention obligation is implied but never stated) and #88 (nothing selects the tenant for a person token).

issues.title: A resource must retain person tokens to issue a step-up or per-call resource token
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
A resource cannot populate a REQUIRED claim of a resource token it is explicitly permitted — and under R3, routinely expected — to issue.

## The conflict

1. **Every resource token needs a person token behind it.** §Person Token: "A resource MUST have verified a person token before it issues a resource token, and MUST challenge with `requirement=person-token` when it has not."

2. **Three of its claims come from that person token.** §Resource Token Structure makes `ps`, `sub`, and `person_token_jti` all REQUIRED, and defines each as copied from the person token the resource verified — `person_token_jti` being "the `jti` of that person token, binding this resource token to it."

3. **But a resource MAY challenge a request that carries an auth token.** §Resource Token: "A resource MAY return `requirement=auth-token` with a new resource token to a request that already includes an auth token — for example, when the request requires a higher level of authorization than the current token provides. Agents MUST be prepared for this step-up authorization at any time."

R3 turns (3) from an occasional step-up into the normal path. §Resource Enforcement: an `r3_per_call` match means "build a per-call proposal and return `AAuth-Requirement` with a resource token referencing it." That challenge happens at call time, on a request that by definition carries an auth token — the agent needed one to reach enforcement at all.

At that moment the agent is presenting an auth token. §Auth Token Structure gives it `ps` and `sub`, but **no `person_token_jti`** — the claim is not in the auth token's required or optional list. The resource has two of the three values it needs and no defined way to obtain the third.

## Three readings, all consistent with the current text

- **The resource retains a record of every person token it verifies**, keyed so it can recover the `jti` later. This makes "MUST have verified" mean "at any point in the past", and hands every resource a storage requirement the specification never states.
- **The resource challenges `requirement=person-token` again** before it can challenge for the step-up. This makes "MUST have verified" mean "on this request", and costs an extra round trip on *every* per-call invocation.
- **The auth token's `ps`/`sub` are meant to suffice for a step-up**, and `person_token_jti` is conditional in a way §Resource Token Structure does not say.

The first is the only reading that keeps `per-call` usable for unattended work. §Operation Access Annotations describes `per-call` as how "an agent planning unattended work identifies the operations that will block on a person"; if every per-call invocation additionally forces a person-token round trip, the extra latency lands on exactly the operations that are already the expensive ones. The reference implementation takes this reading: it keeps a record per `(ps, sub, agent key, mission)` with a TTL equal to the person token's own `exp`, and recovers the `jti` from it when building a per-call or step-up resource token.

## This is #87 arriving at the other party

#87 is the same unstated-persistence problem on the PS side: §Resource Token Verification step 6 requires a PS to "look up the person token identified by `person_token_jti` among those it issued", which silently makes every PS stateful about issued tokens.

This issue is the resource-side mirror. One person token now implies retained state at **both** ends of its life — the PS that issued it and the resource that verified it — and the document states neither. That symmetry suggests the fix belongs in one place covering both parties, rather than two separate paragraphs in two separate sections: what each party retains, for how long, and keyed by what.

## Knock-on for mission stripping

`person_token_jti` exists so the PS can detect mission stripping. §Resource Token Verification: "Binding the resource token to one person token by `jti` is what makes mission stripping detectable. A resource cannot drop `mission_s256` and present the result as an unscoped request, because the PS resolves the person token it actually issued and compares."

Under the retention reading, a resource replays a `jti` from its own record rather than from a token in hand. The PS's check still passes and the property still holds — but only because the resource kept the record honestly, pairing the `jti` with the `mission_s256` that person token actually carried. A resource that retained a `jti` while losing track of which mission it belonged to could pair a mission-bearing `jti` with a stripped resource token and the PS's comparison would catch it, which is the desired outcome; a resource that kept several records and picked the wrong one produces a spurious rejection. Whatever text resolves this should say that the retained record is the whole tuple, not the `jti` alone.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
## Proposed resolution (from the document author)

**The claim names the `jti` of whatever credential the resource verified on the request that produced the resource token — not specifically a person token. Rename it accordingly.**

Today `person_token_jti` hardcodes one credential type into a claim whose job is more general: to name the credential the resource had in hand, so the recipient can resolve it and compare. On a first authorization that credential is a person token. On a step-up or an R3 per-call challenge it is an auth token. The claim should say "the thing I verified", and the resource should always have one, because -11 already requires it.

This dissolves the issue rather than answering the three readings — the question "how does the resource recover a `jti` it no longer holds" stops arising, because it names the `jti` of the credential in its hand.

### Why an auth token works as the carrier

§Auth Token Structure carries `ps`, `sub`, `mission_s256`, and `tenant` — all four of the claims §Resource Token Verification step 6 compares.

§Person Token Structure carries `sub`, `mission_s256`, and `tenant`, but **not** `ps`; its `iss` is the PS. So for this particular check an auth token is a strictly *richer* carrier than a person token, stating `ps` explicitly where a person token only implies it through its issuer. Generalizing the claim is not a widening that has to be defended — the case being added is the better-specified of the two.

### The anti-stripping property is preserved

The mechanism is unchanged: the recipient resolves a token **it issued** under the named `jti` and compares the same four claims. What made the property work was never that the credential was a person token; it was that the recipient could resolve the token authoritatively rather than take the resource's word for the claims.

`(iss, jti)` identifies a token within an issuer's namespace — the rule -10 established for revocation ("A `jti` is unique only within the namespace of the issuer that minted it... Recipients maintaining revocation state MUST key it by `(iss, jti)`"). Here the recipient *is* the issuer, so the `jti` alone suffices and the pair is already the document's established way of naming a token.

### It improves the four-party case

Step 6 currently gives the AS a materially weaker check than the PS:

> A PS MUST look up the person token identified by `person_token_jti` among those it issued, and MUST verify that `ps`, `sub`, `mission_s256`, and `tenant` match that token exactly... An AS MUST verify that `ps` names the PS that sent the token request.

The asymmetry is forced: the resource token names a token the **PS** issued, which the AS has no way to resolve, so the AS is left checking a routing fact instead of comparing claims.

Under the generalized rule a step-up in four-party names an auth token **the AS issued itself**. The AS can then perform the same full comparison the PS does. The first authorization in four-party still names a PS-issued person token and keeps the weaker check, so this does not close the asymmetry entirely — but it closes it exactly where R3 per-call operates, which is the case this issue is about, and per-call is the path where the check runs most often.

## Two constraints on the fix

**The name cannot be bare `jti`.** The resource token already defines its own `jti` for replay detection, audit, and revocation. The new claim needs a distinct name. `presented_jti` reads well — "presents" is the document's own verb for what an agent does with a credential via `Signature-Key` (§Person Token Usage, §Auth Token Usage), so the name says which of the two tokens in play it refers to.

**Scope it to credentials carrying the person's identity** — a person token or an auth token, not an agent token. An agent token has no `sub` and no `mission_s256`, so naming one would leave step 6 comparing nothing: the anti-stripping property would evaporate silently rather than fail loudly, which is the worst failure mode for a defence of this kind. -11 already forbids issuing a resource token without a verified person token behind it (§Person Token: "A resource MUST have verified a person token before it issues a resource token"), so the restriction costs nothing that is currently legal.

## Knock-on: step 6 needs rewording in the same edit

Step 6 is phrased for one credential type — "look up the person token identified by `person_token_jti` among those it issued". Generalized, the recipient looks up whichever token it issued under that `jti`, whatever its type.

Worth doing as part of this change rather than after: once both PS and AS resolve a token they issued and compare the same four claims, the PS/AS split in the step's last sentence may collapse into a single rule, with the AS's weaker `ps`-names-the-sender check surviving only as the fallback for a first authorization in four-party, where the named token is not the AS's. That is a simpler step 6 than the one there now, and leaving it phrased around person tokens would hide the simplification.

## Relationship to #87

#87 is the PS-side retention obligation and is **not** resolved by this. A PS still has to resolve a token it issued, so it still needs the record, and the retention floor, error-code, and keying questions in #87 all stand.

What changes is that the problem stops being symmetric. Under the current text both parties need retention; under this proposal only the issuer does — which is the party that already has a reason to keep issuance records, and the only one that can resolve a token authoritatively. The resource is out of it entirely.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body:
## Closing: the premise is wrong

Worth saying plainly rather than closing quietly, because three implementations built person-token retention and none of them had to. The ergonomics push that way; the document does not require it. The issue asserted that a resource is forced into unstated retention, and that is not so.

Three things dissolve it.

### 1. A resource may simply re-challenge

This is the correction that matters most, and the issue as filed did not consider it.

On a step-up or per-call invocation carrying an auth token, a resource that has no person token in hand can answer `requirement=person-token`. The agent presents one on the retry, and the resource mints the resource token from the credential it now holds. Two round trips, zero retention, fully conformant against the text as it stands today.

The issue listed this as its second reading and dismissed it on cost — "an extra round trip on every per-call invocation". But cost is not conformance. Retention is an **optimisation that saves a round trip**, and a resource is free to decline it. That makes the three readings not a genuine ambiguity but a choice the document already permits, with one branch cheaper than the other. Nothing is unstated; nothing is forced.

### 2. `presented_jti` covers the rest

The proposal above generalizes the claim to name whatever credential the resource verified on the request that produced the resource token.

The supporting fact is stronger in -11 than it was: §Auth Token Structure makes `sub` a **REQUIRED** payload claim. `scope` is optional, and the older "one of `sub` or `scope`" rule is gone from the document entirely. So an auth token carries `ps` + `sub` + `cnf` — everything a person token carries for this purpose, plus authorization.

A per-call challenge therefore arrives on a request already bearing a credential the resource can name. It names *that* token's `jti`. No retention, and no extra round trip either — so the optimisation in (1) is available without the storage that appeared to be its price.

### 3. #92 removes the situation entirely

For the case that prompted this issue, a resource that defers with `202` and holds the invocation never lets go of the credential context in the first place. There is no gap to bridge, because the resource never released the call.

## What survives

**#87 stands unchanged.** The *PS* genuinely must retain the person tokens it issued — it is the only party that can resolve one authoritatively, and the document still never says so, sets no floor, and does not distinguish an absent record from mismatched claims. Closing this issue does not touch any of that.

What it does change is the shape of the problem. Under this issue's framing, persistence was symmetric: both ends of a person token's life needed unstated storage. It is not symmetric. Only the issuer retains, which is the party that already keeps issuance records for revocation and audit. That is a **simplification of #87, not a resolution of it** — the retention floor, the error-code split, and the keying question all remain open there.

**The tuple point is absorbed.** This issue ended by arguing that a retained record must be the whole tuple rather than the `jti` alone, so a resource cannot pair a mission-bearing `jti` with a stripped resource token. Under `presented_jti` that is structural rather than an obligation on the resource: the recipient resolves a token **it** issued and compares all four claims against its own record. The resource holds nothing to get wrong.

Closing as resolved by analysis rather than by a change. Nothing in the drafts needs editing for this issue; `presented_jti` proceeds on its own merits, and #92 on its own.

issues.title: R3 operation access annotations cannot express two common cases
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Implementing operation access annotations in a reference resource turned up two things the annotation vocabulary cannot say. Both generalize well beyond that resource. Framing them as expressiveness gaps rather than proposing wire syntax, because the fix for either interacts with §Applying Annotations in a way that needs deciding first.

## Part 1 — there is no value meaning "no AAuth credential required"

§Access Mode Annotation takes one of `agent-token`, `person-token`, `auth-token`, or `per-call`. The resource-wide `access_mode` in AAuth Protocol has the same floor. The lowest expressible value is still a requirement.

But every resource serves operations that require nothing. `/.well-known/aauth-resource.json` and `/.well-known/jwks.json` are the universal case — they have to be fetchable before any credential exists, since they are how an agent learns which credentials the resource takes and how to verify what it issues. Discovery necessarily precedes authentication.

Unannotated, those operations inherit the resource-wide `access_mode` (§Applying Annotations: "An operation with no access mode annotation takes the resource's `access_mode`"). So a resource declaring `access_mode: auth-token` advertises its own metadata document as requiring an auth token. An agent planning against the vocabulary is told it needs a credential to fetch the document that tells it which credentials exist.

The practical damage is bounded — the well-known paths are fetched by convention, not by reading an annotation, and annotations are advisory anyway. But it bites for any *ordinary* operation that is deliberately open: a public search endpoint, a status or health operation, a price list, a rate-limit probe. The resource has no way to publish "this one is free", and an agent that trusts the annotation does an authorization round trip it never needed.

## Part 2 — the requirement can depend on the parameters, and the slot is per-operation

The reference resource has a single operation whose credential requirement varies with how it is called:

- no `?scope=` — returns the agent's own identity, needs only an agent token
- `?scope=` present — needs a person token, because it is now naming a person
- once an auth token has been issued — that is what the agent presents

One annotation cannot say that. The annotation slot is attached to the operation, and the operation is one operation in every vocabulary that describes it: one MCP tool, one OpenAPI Operation Object.

This is not exotic. Any operation whose credential requirement varies with what it is asked for has the shape, and `?scope=`-style parameters that widen what is returned are common. The alternative — splitting one operation into three so each can carry its own annotation — distorts the API description to work around the annotation format, and §Operation Identifier Scope's uniqueness rules make that a real cost rather than a cosmetic one.

### This is not `per-call`

The two look adjacent and are different.

`per-call` says no credential held in advance is sufficient: the resource challenges every invocation, builds a proposal from that call's concrete parameters, and the resulting grant is consumed by that one call. It is about authorizing **specific parameter values** — this recipient, this amount, this record.

Part 2 is about which credential **tier** applies, where the parameters select the tier and each tier is then a normal reusable grant. `?scope=profile` needs a person token; having obtained one, the agent reuses it. Nothing is consumed and nothing is per-invocation.

An operation could plausibly be both: parameters select the tier, and within the top tier every call is still challenged.

## What makes either awkward to fix

§Applying Annotations sets two rules that any answer has to work with:

> **Annotations are sparse.** An operation with no access mode annotation takes the resource's `access_mode`.

> **An annotation replaces the default rather than intersecting with it.** A `person-token` annotation on a resource declaring `access_mode: auth-token` lowers the requirement for that operation.

"Replaces" is well-defined for one value. Anything that lets an operation carry several modes — a list, a conditional, a parameter-keyed map — has to say what replacement means when there is more than one value. Does the set replace the default wholesale? Does the *lowest* member replace it, with the rest as escalation the agent should expect? Does an agent that does not understand the extended form fall back to the resource-wide default, or to some designated member? That question has to be answered before syntax is worth discussing, and it is the same question for both parts, since Part 1 is arguably just "the set may include a value below `agent-token`".

## What the reference resource did

Worth recording, because it shows the current text working as intended even while incomplete.

The resource declares `access_mode: agent-token` — its true minimum, not its maximum. That matters because of AAuth Protocol's onboarding step 3: "If `access_mode` is `auth-token` and the agent has no PS, it cannot complete that flow and SHOULD skip the resource." Declaring the higher mode would tell a PS-less agent to skip a resource that would have served it perfectly well on its agent token.

And it publishes **no** annotation at all, because §Applying Annotations says "A resource whose operations all work the same way annotates nothing" — and by the annotation's own vocabulary, its one operation does work one way. There is no second value to distinguish it from. The text is followed exactly and the result still under-describes the resource, which is the clearest statement of the gap.

issues.title: Per-call authorization: let a resource defer with 202, and make the grant single-use
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
A design proposal. It spans both documents: the `202` deferral is an AAuth Protocol change, the single-use requirement and the consequences for proposal storage are R3.

## The gap it starts from

**Single-use is stated only descriptively, never normatively.**

R3 §Access Mode Annotation says of `per-call`:

> `per-call` is not a fourth rung on that ladder. It says that no credential held in advance is sufficient: the resource challenges every invocation, builds a proposal from that call's parameters, and **the grant that results is consumed by that one call.**

But the normative text is R3 §Per-Call Proposals, step 3, and it does not say that:

> **Enforced retry.** The agent retries the actual call with the per-call auth token. The resource recovers the proposal from its store via `r3_s256` and MUST verify that the agent's actual parameters match the approved proposal. For any parameter represented as a digest, the resource MUST verify that `BASE64URL(SHA-256(presented-value))` equals the stored `s256`. If anything differs, the resource MUST reject the call. An approval to email one recipient cannot be replayed **against another**.

Every requirement there is about parameters *differing*. The closing sentence rules out replay against a different recipient and is silent on replay against the same one. As written, an agent may present the same per-call auth token repeatedly with byte-identical parameters and every call succeeds until `exp` — one approval, N identical emails. Nothing in step 3 is violated, because nothing differs.

"Consumed by that one call" is the intent. It is in the prose that explains the access mode, not in the section that specifies behaviour.

## The proposal

**A resource MAY answer any `requirement=auth-token` with a `202 Accepted`** carrying `Location`, `Retry-After`, and the `AAuth-Requirement` with its resource token — **holding the invocation** rather than making the agent retry it. The agent obtains the auth token as it does today and completes at the pending URL, presenting the auth token via `Signature-Key` exactly as it would have on the API call.

Not restricted to per-call. Any authorization challenge.

401-retry remains valid, and which to use is the resource's choice. A resource with no store must be able to stay stateless and conformant — the same reason `authorization_endpoint` is OPTIONAL ("When absent, the resource issues resource tokens and interaction requirements via `401` responses").

## This is not a new pattern

AAuth Protocol §Interaction Response already specifies this exact shape, for resource-hosted interaction:

> The agent then holds two pending URLs: the resource's original `Location` (from the resource's `202`) and the PS's relay `Location`. The **resource's** pending URL is authoritative for completion.

A resource already returns a `202` with its own pending URL, the agent already holds two, and the resource's is already authoritative. §Resource-Initiated Interaction is the flow that uses it, for "a proxy's OAuth bootstrap page or a merchant's payment-confirmation page". Agents that support `interaction` have implemented this.

The proposal extends machinery that exists, for interaction, to authorization. It is the same state machine with a different requirement in the header.

## What it buys

**The class-grant vs per-call discriminator disappears.** Today a per-call auth token and a class-grant auth token have the same claim shape. R3 §Auth Token Extensions makes `r3_uri`, `r3_s256`, and `r3_granted` REQUIRED on both, and the per-call flow says the AS "issues a per-call auth token that echoes the proposal's `r3_uri`/`r3_s256` and lists the now-approved operation in `r3_granted`". A resource therefore cannot tell from the claims which kind it holds; it must resolve `r3_s256` against its store to find out — a lookup on **every** call, including class-grant calls that need no document at all. That contradicts R3's own §Resource Enforcement claim that "No token introspection or R3 document fetch is needed at enforcement time." Under `202` the **URL** is the discriminator: a token arriving at a pending URL is by construction a per-call completion, and a token arriving at a normal endpoint is by construction not.

**Parameter re-verification is eliminated, not simplified.** The resource never released the parameters — it held the call. Step 3's key-for-key comparison plus digest re-hashing is the most error-prone requirement in R3, and it evaporates rather than getting easier.

**Single-use becomes inherent.** The pending record is consumed by completion. There is no second thing to present the token to.

**The agent cannot get the retry wrong**, because it does not reconstruct the call. Today a mismatch between the call the agent proposed and the call it retries is an agent bug that surfaces as an authorization rejection.

**No new exposure.** Digest parameters exist so the PS and the AS never see the values (R3 §Large and Sensitive Payloads). The resource always held them. Holding them a few seconds longer changes nothing about who sees what.

## What it requires

**Single-use MUST, on both paths.** This is the part that should land regardless of whether the `202` half is adopted. Single-use is a property of the grant, not of the delivery mechanism — otherwise one approval means different things depending on which status code the resource happened to choose, which is not something a person approving a call can reason about. It is cheap either way: under `202` the pending record is consumed by completion; under `401` the resource marks consumed the proposal record it already stores in order to verify parameters at all.

**Idempotent completion.** The bare version has a real failure mode: the resource executes the call, the response is lost in transit, the agent retries, and single-use turns a successful send into a refusal — with the agent unable to distinguish "not sent" from "sent, receipt lost". The pending record must move to *completed, with the result*, and be retained briefly, so that a duplicate completion is answered from the record rather than re-executed or rejected. The pending URL is a natural idempotency key, which is one more thing the `202` path gets for free and the `401` path has to construct.

**Two independent clocks.** Resource tokens "SHOULD NOT have a lifetime exceeding 5 minutes" and human approval routinely takes longer. The document already names this and already answers it: "If a resource token expires before the PS presents it to the AS (e.g., because user interaction was required), the agent MUST obtain a fresh resource token from the resource and submit a new token request to the PS." Under `202` that answer gets strictly better — the pending record survives independently of the resource token, so the resource re-mints against the call it is still holding. No re-authorization, and no lost parameters. Worth stating explicitly, because it is a better answer to a problem the document has already conceded.

**The R3 document is still stored.** This is not a storage saving; the PS and AS fetch `r3_uri` during evaluation regardless. What changes is the document's *lifetime*: today it must outlive the pending call and survive until a retry that may never arrive, so its expiry is decoupled from anything. Under `202` its lifetime unifies with the pending record. One reference implementation was pushed into a 24-hour hash index alongside a 15-minute body plus a `proposal_expired` error precisely because the retry window and the proposal window are independent today.

## Why the generalization is the simplifying move

Restricting `202` to per-call would make it a special case with its own rules. Allowing it for any `requirement=auth-token` gives one rule —

> a resource MAY deliver an auth-token requirement as a `401` the agent retries, or as a `202` it completes

— and one agent code path, which is the deferred-response loop the agent already runs for interaction. Per-call then needs no special handling at all; it is the case where a resource has the strongest reason to choose `202`, not a different mechanism.

## Related

#90 — a resource must retain person tokens to issue a step-up or per-call resource token. That issue's retention question is reshaped by this proposal: a resource holding the invocation still has the credential context in hand at the moment it completes, rather than having to recover it from a record after a round trip it did not participate in.

issues.title: Metadata: optional property advertising accepted signature algorithms
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Problem

Discovery of a party's accepted signature algorithms is currently in-band only: `Accept-Signature-Alg` on the error response (signature-key) after an `unsupported_algorithm` failure. That recovers in one round trip, but it is reactive — an agent choosing which key to *enroll* (hardware ES256 vs Ed25519, or a future ML-DSA key) has no way to learn the accepted set before first contact, and enrolling the wrong key type on hardware costs a user interaction.

## Proposal

Add an OPTIONAL property to the common metadata fields (§common-metadata-fields), published by any party that serves metadata:

```json
"accept_signature_algs": ["Ed25519", "ES256", "RS256"]
```

Semantics identical to the `Accept-Signature-Alg` response header (signature-key §accept-signature-alg): fully-specified identifiers from the IANA JOSE registry, stating exactly the set the party's verifier accepts — neither a subset nor a superset. A party MAY omit it for the same disclosure-risk reasons it MAY omit the header. One list per party, not per endpoint — every inbound signature goes through the same verification path.

## Naming

- `accept_signature_algs` — mirrors the `Accept-Signature-Alg` header this duplicates out-of-band; makes the exact-set equivalence obvious. **Preferred.**
- `signature_alg_values_supported` — RFC 8414 convention, but 8414/OIDC `*_alg_values_supported` fields are all per-use (client auth, request objects, id_token); this property is deliberately not per-use, so borrowing that convention may mislead.

## Notes

- Hellō person server is provisionally publishing `accept_signature_algs` in `aauth-person.json` on beta to exercise the field; rename follows whatever the spec decides.
- Interaction with §signature-algorithms: Ed25519 is MUST-support for every party, so the property can never usefully omit Ed25519; its value is advertising the *additional* algorithms.

issues.title: Rename person_token_jti — the credential it names is not always a person token
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## The name is wrong

`person_token_jti` is a REQUIRED resource token claim, defined in §Resource Token Structure as:

> `person_token_jti`: The `jti` of that person token, binding this resource token to it

The name asserts that the credential the resource verified was a person token. That is true on the first resource token of a grant and false thereafter.

**A step-up resource token follows an auth token.** §Resource Access and Resource Tokens permits a resource to return `requirement=auth-token` with a fresh resource token to a request that already carries an auth token — nested authorization, and under AAuth Budgets, an exhausted budget. R3 makes it the normal path rather than an occasional one: a `per-call` match builds its proposal at call time, on a request that by definition already carries an auth token.

At that moment the credential in `Signature-Key` is an `aa-auth+jwt`. The resource is naming a person token it verified at some earlier point, recovered from its own retained record (#90). Calling the claim `person_token_jti` describes where the value originally came from, not what the resource just checked, and it reads to an implementer as "copy this from the token in your hand" — which is exactly the reading #90 shows does not work.

## Proposal

Rename to **`caller_jti`**.

"Caller" is the vocabulary the drafts already use for the party on the other end of a request, and it stays true across every case: the claim names the `jti` of the AAuth credential that established who the caller is, whichever type that credential was.

Alternatives considered and why not:

- `subject_token_jti` — precedent in RFC 8693, but that term means the token being exchanged, and nothing is being exchanged here
- `presented_jti` / `verified_jti` — accurate but say nothing about whose identity was established
- keeping `person_token_jti` and narrowing the definition — leaves the misleading name in place while the text does the correcting

## Say what it is for, where the reader meets it

Separately from the rename: the claim's purpose is not visible at the point of introduction. Today a reader meets it as one line in a claims list, and the reason it exists — that it is what makes **mission stripping detectable** — appears in a design rationale section a long way away:

> Binding the resource token to one person token by `jti` is what makes mission stripping detectable. A resource cannot drop `mission_s256` and present the result as an unscoped request, because the PS resolves the person token it actually issued and compares. Comparing the claims alone would not suffice: an agent running concurrent missions holds several person tokens for the same resource, so "the person token for this agent and resource" does not identify one.

That argument is correct and it is the answer to the first question a reviewer asks about the claim. It should appear where the claim is defined, in a sentence, with the rationale section as the long form.

This is not a normative gap — the binding is fully specified and the PS-side check in §Resource Token Verification step 6 is exactly right. It is a discoverability gap: in the August 2026 office hours the binding was raised as something the spec still needed to add, by a reader who had gone through the person token material. If it did not land there, the placement is wrong.

## Scope

- Rename the claim in §Resource Token Structure and §Resource Token Verification
- State the binding's purpose at the definition
- Check the IANA JWT claim registration
- Note the interaction with #87 and #90, which are the same claim's retention story at each end

issues.title: Relate AAuth tokens to the OIDC ID token — readers are deriving this themselves and getting cnf wrong
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## The audience builds this bridge themselves, badly

In the August 2026 office hours, working out what a person token *is* took the room to this on its own:

> Person token is a strict subset of an ID token (just `sub`). Auth token is a superset — all the ID token claims plus authorization claims.

That framing appears nowhere in the specification. It is close enough to be useful and wrong in the part that matters, and both facts are the specification's problem.

Close enough: the person token really is the identity assertion with the authorization stripped out, and relating it to an ID token is the fastest way to convey that to anyone who has implemented OIDC — which is most of the people we need.

Wrong where it counts: "just `sub`" drops `cnf`. A person token is bound to the agent's key and is not a bearer credential, which is the entire security difference from an ID token. It also drops `aud` being a single resource, and the 1-hour cap. If that is the summary a reader leaves with after a full session on the topic, §Person Token Structure is leading with the wrong material — a flat list of claims, with the properties that distinguish it buried among the routine ones.

## Proposal

A short subsection relating AAuth's tokens to OIDC, for readers arriving from it. Roughly:

| | ID Token | Person token | Auth token |
|---|---|---|---|
| Asserts | who signed in | which person the agent acts for | what is authorized |
| Audience | the relying party | one resource | one resource |
| Presentation | bearer | proof of possession, `cnf` bound to the agent key | proof of possession |
| Freshness | `nonce`, ties to one sign-in | short lifetime, ≤ 1 hour | short lifetime, ≤ 1 hour |
| Authorization | none | none | `scope`, `account`, `budget` |

with prose on the three things an OIDC reader will otherwise get wrong:

1. **It is not a bearer token.** `cnf` binds it to the key that signs the request. An intercepted person token is useless without the key.
2. **There is no `nonce` and no sign-in event.** An ID token attests that a person authenticated just now to the RP. A person token attests that this PS knows this person and this agent acts for them. Different claim, and it is why there is nothing to replay-protect in the OIDC sense.
3. **`sub` is directed and stable across agents.** Same value for that person at that resource whichever agent presents it, different value at every other resource.

Related: #5 (closed) asked for OIDC/OAuth interop patterns generally. This is narrower — not how to interoperate, but how to *read* AAuth if OIDC is what you already know.

Companion issue on the site side: aauth-dev/www.

issues.title: Person token: state the assurance floor — the name implies proofing the protocol does not do
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## The claim the name makes

Raised by Wayne Chang in the August 2026 office hours: **"person token" implies identity assurance the protocol does not guarantee.** The protocol proves "the same entity again," not verified legal identity.

He is right, and the specification's own wording invites the misreading. §Person Token opens:

> A person token is a PS-issued JWT that identifies the person an agent acts for to a single resource.

"Identifies the person" is exactly the phrase that, to a reader coming from identity assurance work — NIST 800-63, mDL, eIDAS — means an identity was proofed. Nothing in the specification says what standard, if any, the PS applied before minting the token, and nothing says a resource may not assume one.

What the protocol actually delivers:

- a `sub` that is stable and directed for one person at one resource
- an assertion that this PS asserts this agent acts for that person
- a key binding through `cnf`

What it does not deliver, and never claims to in normative text:

- any identity proofing level
- any statement that the person is a natural person, or is who they say they are
- anything a resource can rely on for an age check, a residency check, or a regulated onboarding

The gap matters because the natural next question is exactly the one that followed it in that session: can an mDL claim ride in the token? (Filed separately.) A resource that wired an age gate to a person token because the name promised a person would be building on nothing.

## Proposal

State the assurance floor where the token is introduced. Something to the effect of:

> A person token asserts that its issuer recognizes this person and that this agent acts for them. It carries no statement about how the person server established the person's identity, and a resource MUST NOT treat it as evidence of identity proofing, of legal identity, or of any assurance level. What it guarantees is continuity: the same `(iss, sub)` is the same person at this resource over time. A resource requiring assurance beyond continuity obtains it out of band or through claims a person server explicitly asserts.

Plus a Security Considerations subsection on the difference between continuity and proofing, since "same entity again" is genuinely sufficient for most resource access and the specification should say so confidently rather than leave the reader to assume it is a weaker version of something else.

## The name

Worth deciding explicitly rather than by default. `person token` is short, it reads well against `agent token` and `auth token`, and it is now in the wire format as `aa-person+jwt`, the PS metadata as `person_token_endpoint`, the access mode as `person-token`, and an `AAuth-Requirement` value. Renaming is expensive and I do not think the name is wrong — the token *is* about a person, in contrast to the agent.

My read is: keep the name, and remove the ambiguity with text, because the objection is to an implied assurance claim and that can be denied in one paragraph. But the objection came from someone who works in exactly this area, so the decision should be recorded rather than assumed.

issues.title: State a position on verifiable credentials in auth tokens (wallet claims, assurance levels)
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Where it came from

Raised by Wayne Chang in the August 2026 office hours, and left unresolved when he had to drop. AAuth has no stated position on verifiable credentials, and the question arrives unprompted from anyone working on wallets.

## The use case

An agent buys something age-gated on the person's behalf. The resource needs proof of two things — over 21, and California residency — and the person holds an mDL that can prove both. Today the auth token can say what the agent may do and cannot say anything about the person beyond a directed `sub`.

The related observations from that discussion:

- **Assurance is not one level.** Buying alcohol and claiming a benefit sit at different points, and a resource should be able to state which it needs rather than take whatever arrives.
- **Device binding raises assurance.** An mDL presented from a FIPS 140 secure element is a stronger statement than one presented from software, and that distinction is meaningful to a verifier.
- **The presentation problem is the hard part.** A wallet presentation protocol assumes a person at a device who can be prompted. An agent acting unattended has neither.

## The direction discussed

The person server issues the auth token with a wallet-derived claim embedded. The resource is the verifier; the person server is the conduit to the wallet. That fits the shape AAuth already has — the PS is the only party with the person relationship and the only one that can prompt them, and it is already the party that runs an interaction when a decision needs a human.

It also raises questions this document has not answered:

- What does the resource ask for, and where? Presumably alongside `scope` at the authorization endpoint, in the resource token, and narrowed down the same chain — but a credential request is not a scope and the narrowing rule may not transfer.
- What does the PS return? A claim it asserts on its own authority after verifying a presentation, or the presentation itself passed through? The first makes the PS a trusted issuer for something it did not issue; the second makes the resource implement wallet verification.
- How does a resource state the assurance it needs, and how does a PS state what it applied? This is #97 arriving from the other side: that issue says a person token asserts no proofing, and this one is the mechanism by which proofing could be asserted when a resource genuinely needs it.
- What happens when the person is not reachable? The PS already has `user_unreachable` and the deferred-response machinery, so probably nothing new — worth confirming rather than assuming.

## What this issue is asking for

Not a mechanism yet. A **stated position**, so that the question stops being answered ad hoc in meetings:

1. Whether credential presentation is in scope for the protocol, a companion document, or out of scope entirely. My read is companion document — it is a coherent piece of work with its own audience, and folding it into the protocol would hold the protocol open.
2. If companion or out of scope, name the attachment point in the protocol anyway. A sentence saying claims about the person may be carried in the auth token and that a separate document defines how they get there is worth more than silence, because silence reads as "nobody has thought about this."
3. Related prior art to look at: Ramp's agent cards were flagged in the same session as relevant to PCI-free agent payments, which is the same shape of problem — a credential the agent must not hold.

Related: #97 (assurance floor), #48 (DID-binding profile for person servers).

issues.title: Move the person token endpoint into §8; keep the token structure in §6
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Feedback from Jared Hanson on the editor's draft.

The person token endpoint is documented in §6.1. Every other PS endpoint is in §8 Person Server: auth token (§8.1), permission (§8.4), audit (§8.5), interaction (§8.6). `person_token_endpoint` sits alongside all of them in the PS metadata document (§13.11.2). Someone implementing a PS has to read §6.1 and §8, and nothing in §6 signals that the endpoint just described is one the PS provides.

Agent tokens already have the split being asked for here. §5.2.1 describes acquisition abstractly and defers the mechanism; §5.2.2 defines the structure. The PS-side request an agent actually makes is §8.1.3. Structure is defined where the credential is introduced, the endpoint where the role that serves it is defined.

**Proposal**

Keep §6 Person Token: the recitals about what the token does and does not assert, structure (§6.2), usage (§6.3), verification (§6.4). Move §6.1 Person Token Endpoint into §8 — adjacent to §8.1 PS Token Endpoint — and leave a pointer in §6 the way §5.2.1 points out of §5.

Two things that need adjusting with the move:

- §8's opening sentence is "This section defines how agents obtain authorization from their person server." A person token carries no authorization, so the framing has to widen to "what a PS serves to agents" rather than authorization specifically.
- §4.4.2 says "The PS provides three governance endpoints" and lists permission, audit, and interaction. Counting `auth_token_endpoint`, `person_token_endpoint`, `mission_endpoint`, and `mission_control_endpoint`, a PS serves seven. If §8 is meant to be the one place a PS implementer reads, it should open with the full endpoint list.

comments.author: dickhardt
comments.body: @jaredhanson filed from your feedback — the endpoint placement point is yours. Flagging the two knock-on items I added (§8's intro framing, and the endpoint count in §4.4.2) in case you disagree with either.

issues.title: Lingering agent-token references where the person token is now authoritative
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
Second half of Jared Hanson's feedback — lingering references to agent tokens that should now be person tokens. He said he would post his own list once he confirms it; these are the ones I found while checking. Companion to #103.

**The rule the draft states three times**

- §5.2.2, on the agent token's `ps` claim: "The PS of an issued authorization is the `iss` of the person token the resource verified (#person-token-structure), not this claim."
- §7.8.1, on the resource token's `ps` claim: "The `iss` of the person token the resource verified — the person server whose namespace `sub` belongs to"
- §4.6: "The `ps` claim in the agent token tells the resource the agent has a person server, before the resource has anything else to go on. The PS a resource acts on is the `iss` of the person token it verifies"

**Three places in §7 that still route on the agent token**

1. §7 intro: "If the resource has no AS but the agent has a PS (`ps` claim in agent token): `aud` = PS URL (three-party)"
2. §7.2 intro: "The resource can handle authorization itself, or it can issue a resource token when the resource has an AS or the agent token includes a `ps` claim."
3. §7.2.2: "If the resource has no AS but the agent has a PS (`ps` claim): `aud` = PS URL (three-party)"

All three set `aud` from the agent token. They should read from the person token the resource verified. The paragraph immediately above (1) already says a resource MUST have verified a person token before it issues a resource token — at that point the resource holds `iss` and does not need the hint. The agent token's `ps` claim decides whether challenging with `requirement=person-token` is worth the round trip; it does not decide the audience.

**Related, §7.1**

> An agent with no person server cannot obtain a person token and so cannot use the authorization endpoint. It calls the resource's endpoints directly and takes whatever the resource challenges with — identity-based access (#requirement-agent-token) or resource-managed authorization (#resource-managed-auth). The `401` path (#requirement-auth-token) is reached with an agent token as before.

The last sentence contradicts the section it is in. A `requirement=auth-token` 401 carries a resource token, §7 says a resource MUST NOT issue one without a verified person token and MUST challenge with `requirement=person-token` instead, and an agent with no PS has nowhere to redeem a resource token anyway. The sentence should be dropped or replaced with the statement that identity access and resource-managed access are the whole of what is available without a PS.

**Related, §8.1.3**

The subsection is titled "Agent Token Request" but is the request for an *auth* token — the agent presents its agent token there, and since #75 the draft has two other agent-presented credentials. Retitle to "Auth Token Request", matching the `auth_token_endpoint` rename in #81.

issues.title: 429 from a resource invocation has no defined semantics — the only 429 in -11 is polling slow_down
issues.author: dickhardt
issues.body:
## Problem

-11 has no way for a resource to say "I am rate limited" as the outcome of an **invocation**.

`429` appears in the draft in exactly one role: `slow_down` in (#polling-error-codes), meaning the agent is polling a pending URL too frequently and should add 5 seconds to its interval. That is a statement about *polling cadence*, not about the resource's capacity to do the work.

There is also no resource error-code table. (#token-endpoint-error-codes) and (#polling-error-codes) are the only two enumerations. A resource that wants to refuse an invocation for capacity reasons has no registered `error` value to put in the RFC 9457 body, and an agent receiving a `429` from a resource endpoint cannot tell whether it means "you are polling too fast" or "this resource cannot serve you right now."

## Why it matters

A proxy resource fronting a third-party API inherits that API's limits. Those limits are frequently scoped to the **OAuth client**, not the calling agent — so every agent using that proxy shares one quota. This changes what the agent should do, and the agent currently has no way to know:

- **Limit is the agent's own** → back off, retry later, the quota recovers because you stopped.
- **Limit is shared across all agents using this resource** → backing off may not help within any useful horizon, because other agents are still consuming it. Retrying is close to useless; the agent should plan around the resource, tell the user, or pick a different resource.

Same status code, same `Retry-After`, opposite correct behaviour.

## Suggested direction

1. **A resource error-code table**, with at least a rate-limit code (`rate_limited` / `too_many_requests`), so the `error` member in the problem+json body is defined for the invocation case rather than borrowed from the polling table.

2. **A scope indicator** — whether the exhausted quota is attributable to this agent, to this user, or shared across the resource's clients. This is the field that makes the response actionable.

3. **Disambiguate `429`.** Either register the invocation meaning explicitly alongside `slow_down`, or use a distinct status for the invocation case. As written, an agent that shares 429 handling between polling and invocation will apply linear polling backoff to a capacity refusal.

4. **`Retry-After` requirements.** State whether it is REQUIRED on a rate-limit refusal and what the agent does when it is absent. Upstreams differ: some send `Retry-After` in seconds, some send a reset timestamp in a proprietary header, some send nothing.

5. **Relationship to `202`.** (#deferred-responses) already lets a resource hold an invocation rather than refuse it, and (#deferred-auth-token) already specifies the replay rule — the resource retains the result and answers a repeat presentation from that result rather than executing twice. A rate-limited invocation looks like a natural fit: hold it, return `202` with `Retry-After`, execute when the window opens. Worth stating explicitly that a resource MAY defer for capacity reasons and that the same replay requirement applies, so implementers do not have to infer it. `Prefer: wait=N` then covers short waits without a round trip.

If (5) is the recommended shape, the guidance is roughly: short wait → hold and defer via `202`; long or shared-quota exhaustion → refuse with the new error code and a scope, so the agent can plan instead of poll.

## Context

Found while designing 429 handling for an AAuth proxy fleet that fronts ~40 third-party APIs (Slack, GitHub, Google, Asana, Calendly, X, Dropbox, …). Each has its own rate-limit dialect, and normalizing them to something an agent can act on ran straight into this gap.
